stem: The WHO definition of impairment is:

options.html: Any loss or abnormality of psychological, physiological or anatomical structure/function
The inability of a person to perform at a satisfactory level in an activity in which they want to succeed
Any loss or abnormality of technical expertise previously possessed by an individual

answer: The correct answer is A. Any loss or abnormality of psychological, physiological or anatomical structure/function. Contrast with disability in Q2 — impairment is just the lack of function.

weekLabel: Week 7 - Approach to MSK, the Spine & the Shoulder Girdle
lecture: Disability, the MSK history & bone structure
lectureMeta: Workbook Q1-Q2, Q68, Q75, Q77. Tests [[01 - Introduction to MSK Anatomy]].
stem: The WHO definition of disability is:

options.html: Any activity that creates an improvement in the ability of an individual to perform, accomplish, or complete an activity in the manner beyond their baseline performance
Any activity limitation that creates a difficulty in the performance, accomplishment, or completion of an activity in the manner or within the range considered normal
The inability to achieve satisfactory performance levels in competitive athletics

answer:
The correct answer is B. Disability is any restriction or lack of ability to perform an activity in the manner or within the range considered normal for a human being.

This is different from impairment (Q1), which is just lack of function. Disability is about the inability to achieve goals because of that lack of function — you can have an impairment, such as a minor limp, that results in no disability at all.

lecture: Disability, the MSK history & bone structure
lectureMeta: Workbook Q1-Q2, Q68, Q75, Q77. Tests [[01 - Introduction to MSK Anatomy]].
stem: _______ cells are responsible for building bone while ________ cells are responsible for reabsorbing bone. These two cells are referred to collectively as the ______________.
answer:
The correct answer is A. Osteoblasts (bone building) + osteoclasts (bone resorbing) = the basic multicellular unit.

Osteoblast vs. osteocyte — the key's own note, worth keeping: osteoblasts produce the non-cellular bone structure (collagen and matrix proteins) and are the major builders of bone tissue. Osteoblasts transform into osteocytes once they surround themselves with bone tissue, at which point the osteocytes maintain and slowly replace bone over time.

lecture: Disability, the MSK history & bone structure
lectureMeta: Workbook Q1-Q2, Q68, Q75, Q77. Tests [[01 - Introduction to MSK Anatomy]].
stem: What are the anatomical regions of long bones from middle to ends?
answer:
The correct answer is D. From middle to ends: diaphysis (middle portion) → metaphysis → growth plate → epiphysis. The epiphysis is covered in articular cartilage.

Note this is the reverse reading of the same sequence that defines the fracture terms in Q19 (diaphyseal vs. metaphyseal vs. intra-articular).

stem: The atlanto-occipital joint allows for _____ and _____ movements like those performed when _____ the head while the atlanto-axial joint allows for ____ movements like those performed when saying _____.
answer: The correct answer is D. Atlanto-occipital = flexion/extension = nodding ("yes"); atlanto-axial = rotation = shaking the head ("no"). The atlanto-occipital joint is a synovial joint between the atlas (C1) and the occipital bone.

stem: In which of the following cases would you order a CT scan of the spine?

options.html: A 40-year-old woman with a 6 week history of what appears to be mechanical pain radiating to the buttocks, that has had only minimal improvement with consistent PT sessions.
A 20-year-old male with morning stiffness in the back that improves with activity, and back pain that worsens nightly.

A 70-year-old woman with back pain radiating down to her right leg and toes for 3 months, despite consistent PT sessions and regular use of Acetaminophen. There is subjective weakness and numbness on the right lateral leg. No bladder, bowel or erectile dysfunction.
a 30-year-old man in a MVC this morning, has severe neck pain despite analgesics. X-rays of C-Spine were normal.

answer:
The correct answer is D. CT is the modality for an occult fracture after trauma with negative plain films — that is the whole point of the question. Each distractor is a different modality:

  • A — this patient may simply benefit from further PT. If PT has been sufficient, the next step is x-ray (more accessible, less radiation) or MRI if suspecting spinal stenosis.
  • B — this is inflammatory back pain (morning stiffness improving with activity, worse at night), which requires MRI if imaging is indicated.
  • C — needs MRI after a long course of therapy, with a presentation consistent with nerve root compression.

stem: The most common levels for disc herniation are:
answer: The correct answer is D. Sources vary on exact locations, but the majority agree that 95% of disc herniations occur in the lumbar region, at L4-L5 or L5-S1. The second most common region is cervical, between C5-C6 or C6-C7.

stem: A 25 y/o olympian gymnast came in after an injury at practice, he had sustained a fall and landed on his back. X-ray showed a fracture in her vertebrae at the thoracic level there are no evidence of any lateral shift or fracture, which type of deformity might he present later?
answer:
The correct answer is C. A vertebral fracture can cause the spine to come closer together, giving a "hump" appearance — and that is especially true at the thoracic level, which is where kyphosis lives.

The distractors are excluded by location or cause: lordosis is lower, at the lumbar section; malformation is usually congenital; scoliosis is a lateral deformity, and the stem explicitly says there is no lateral shift.

stem: Which of the following correctly matches the number of vertebrae with their anatomic region?
answer:
The correct answer is C. 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar.

From Anatomy of the Back & Spinal Cord. The notes' counts are 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, a sacrum of 5 fused segments and a coccyx of 4 fused. C is the only option with both numbers right. The spinal-cord lecture gives a cross-check: there are 8 cervical spinal nerves for 7 cervical vertebrae (C8 exits below C7), whereas the 12 thoracic and 5 lumbar nerves match their vertebrae one-to-one.

  • A fails: cervical is 7, not 4.
  • B fails: it hands the cervical count (7) to the thoracic region; lumbar is 5.
  • D fails: the coccyx is 4 fused segments; 5 is the sacrum.
  • E fails: neither is a single bone's worth of segments - sacrum 5, coccyx 4.

flags.title: The key's own counts are loosely worded
flags.html: The key adds "4 coccyx vertebrae, and 1 sacrum/sacral vertebra" — treating the fused sacrum as a single bone while counting the coccygeal segments separately. Conventionally there are 5 fused sacral and 4 fused coccygeal segments. Option D (coccyx 5) and E (coccyx 1, sacral 1) are both wrong under either count, so the answer is unaffected.

stem: You see a patient in your family clinic who complains of lower back pain. What red flags findings are you looking for on history and physical exam? (Choose 5 answers)
answer:
The correct answers are B, C, G, I, K. Red flags for lower back pain:

  • Night/rest pain ← B
  • Saddle anesthesia ← C
  • Weight loss ← G
  • Incontinence ← I
  • IV drug use ← K
  • advanced age (fragility fracture risk)
  • previous cancer history
  • immunosuppression (HIV, steroids)
  • trauma
  • erectile dysfunction

Note that saddle anesthesia and incontinence together are the cauda equina syndrome pair — the emergency this screen exists to catch.

stem: An elderly man comes to the emergency department complaining of shoulder pain after a fall. Upon physical exam you note decreased range of motion. When you lift his arm vertically above his head and then ask him to slowly lower it back down to his side you note that his arm is controlled at first and then drops abruptly to his side. What is the diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is D. This is the Drop Arm test, a classic test for rotator cuff injury (the other is the empty can test). The arm falls because of a supraspinatus tear.

C is excluded by the manoeuvre itself: with a shoulder dislocation you would not be able to lift the man's arm completely above his head in the first place. See rotator cuff tendinopathy and rotator cuff muscles.

stem: Which ligaments are damaged during a separated or sprung shoulder?
answer:
The correct answer is B. In a typical shoulder separation, the ligaments that may be damaged are the acromioclavicular, the coracoclavicular (trapezoid and conoid) and/or the coracoacromial.

The discriminator across the options is the coracohumeral ligament, which appears in A, C, D and E and is not part of the injury — the trapezoid and conoid are the coracoclavicular ligament, which is what makes B complete.

stem: The anatomical neck of the humerus is located _________ and the surgical neck of the humerus is located ________. The bony landmark between the two heads is called the ________.
answer: The correct answer is B. Anatomical neck = proximal; surgical neck = distal; landmark between = greater tubercle. The surgical neck is much more frequently fractured — which is where its name comes from.

stem: What is it called when there is partial but incomplete separation of joints in the shoulder where joint articulating surfaces are misaligned?
answer:
The correct answer is B. The three real terms, all defined against each other:

  • Apprehension — the fear that the shoulder will subluxate or dislocate, which may prevent full participation in work or sport
  • Subluxation — partial but incomplete dislocation; articulating surfaces misaligned
  • Dislocation — complete separation of the joint's articulating surfaces

"Demi-dislocation" is not a term. See glenohumeral joint.

stem: A 55-year-old man has 3 months of axial low back pain. It is worse when he leans backward and eases when he bends forward. There is no radiation below the knee and his neurological exam is normal. What is the most likely source of his pain?
answer: The correct answer is A. Facetogenic pain is worse in extension (the facets are pushed together) and relieved by flexion, so management is flexion-based physiotherapy and NSAIDs. Discogenic pain is the opposite: axial pain aggravated by forward flexion. No radiation and a normal neuro exam argue against a nerve root.

options.html: Reassure him, most back pain is benign and self-limited
Suggest routine acetaminophen for the next one week then follow up

answer: The correct answer is A. Imaging should always be planned for people with red flag symptoms (young age, fever, night-dominant pain).

stem: You’ve determined that a 72 year old male in your practice most likely have mechanical spine pain. He’s had this pain for about 5 weeks and he feels it is quite severe. There are no red flags. He hasn’t tried anything yet for his pain. What would you suggest to this man?
answer: The correct answer is C. Physical therapy is the mainstay of mechanical spine pain treatment. Most mechanical spine pain will improve over time. Facet injection could be considered after he has tried therapy without sufficient relief. Codeine and other narcotics should be avoided in mechanical spine pain if possible (and again, this man hasn’t yet tried other options like acetaminophen). Surgical referrals are best reserved for axial pain with associated neurological symptoms (and outcomes of surgery for purely axial mechanical pain are typically poor)

stem: A 72-year-old man has burning and tingling in both legs after walking a block. He finds he can walk further leaning on a shopping cart. When he stops, sitting relieves the symptoms, but only after several minutes. Pedal pulses are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is B. Lumbar central stenosis: legs > back, burning/tingling, aggravated by walking and relieved by forward flexion (cart, uphill). Relief with rest is slower than in vascular claudication, which settles within minutes of stopping. It is a nerve root problem (the cord ends at L1) and there are no bowel or bladder features, which separates it from cauda equina.

stem: A 44-year-old man develops back pain radiating down his leg after lifting a box. MRI shows a posterolateral disc herniation at L4-L5. Which finding is most expected?
answer: The correct answer is C. Lumbar nerves exit below their own vertebra, so a posterolateral L4-L5 herniation compresses the L5 root. L5: dorsum of foot (1st-3rd webspace), extension of the great toe. The patellar reflex is L4; plantar flexion, the lateral heel and the Achilles reflex are S1.

stem: A 64-year-old woman has 6 months of worsening clumsiness doing up buttons and an unsteady gait. She has wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles, hyperreflexia in all four limbs and new urinary incontinence. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.html: Nerve conduction studies for carpal tunnel
Physiotherapy with a trial of oral NSAIDs
Cervical MRI and urgent spine referral

answer: The correct answer is D. This is cervical stenosis with cord compression (cervical spondylotic myelopathy): reduced dexterity, intrinsic hand wasting, gait change, urinary symptoms and UMN signs below the level. Unlike lumbar stenosis it is a cord problem, so confirm with MRI and refer urgently for decompression.

stem: A 16-year-old gymnast has low back pain that is worse when she arches her back. Imaging shows a defect of the pars interarticularis of L5 without slippage. What is the diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is E. Spondylolysis is a fracture of the pars interarticularis, typical of young athletes who repeatedly extend the back (gymnasts, football players, weightlifters), and it can progress to spondylolisthesis. Spondylosis is degenerative disc disease plus facet arthropathy. (The review slide labels this entity "spondylosis"; the inherited note calls it spondylolysis, which is the standard term.)

stem: A 73 year old patient comes in complaining of chronic neck and back pain. Over the last 3 months, this seems to be radiating down the right arm into the thumb and index finger. The pain is not severe. She finds that she’s been dropping things lately (she’s broken several dishes!). She’s otherwise well (no significant cardiac or respiratory history, no history of diabetes). She’s noticed an increased frequency of urinary incontinence lately, and has had a UTI ruled out with a urinalysis and culture. Which of the following managements would be most appropriate here?

options.html: Acetaminophen for neck and arm pain
X-ray cervical spine with flexion/extension views

answer: The correct answer is B. Obviously a physical exam may sway you more in one direction than another here, but the critical features here are neck pain, radiation into the arm, loss of dexterity and urinary incontinence. All of these should make you wonder about possible cervical myelopathy, for which an MRI is the most appropriate investigation.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has deep aching shoulder pain. Active range of motion is reduced but passive range is full, and rotator cuff strength is poor. X-ray shows symmetric joint space loss, erosions and osteopenia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is A. Passive ROM separates the two: inflammatory arthritis loses active but not passive motion and has weak cuff muscles, with symmetric joint space, erosions and osteopenia on x-ray (reverse arthroplasty if surgery). Non-inflammatory (OA, post-traumatic) loses both active and passive motion with strength intact and an asymmetric joint space with osteophytes. Adhesive capsulitis has a normal x-ray.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes had several months of shoulder pain, and now the shoulder is stiff. Active and passive motion are globally restricted in every direction. Shoulder x-ray is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is B. Adhesive capsulitis: 40s-50s, diabetes (affects ~20% of patients with diabetes), spontaneous onset, global loss of active AND passive motion, and a normal x-ray. It runs freezing, frozen, thawing. Osteoarthritis also loses passive motion but shows osteophytes and joint space loss; cuff disease preserves passive motion.

answer: The correct answer is C. AC separation follows a fall onto the shoulder (acromion driven down, clavicle up). Grades I-III are managed non-surgically with education, a sling, local analgesia/ice and early exercise; grades IV and V go to surgery.

stem: A 19-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of both shoulders "slipping" with everyday tasks. There was no injury. Exam shows multidirectional laxity and poor scapular motor control. What is the first-line treatment?
answer: The correct answer is D. Atraumatic instability ("born loose") is multidirectional, often bilateral, with poor motor control, and is treated with physiotherapy and muscle strengthening rather than surgery. Traumatic instability ("torn loose") is almost always anterior and is more often treated surgically.

preamble.html: 47-Year-Old Rower. The case sits in the lecture's "AC Joint Instability: Separation" section. His shoulder X-ray is shown.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.html: Surgical stabilisation of the AC joint
Education, ice, a sling and early motion
Inferior capsular shift of the shoulder

answer:
The correct answer is B. The case's own caption gives his treatment as "education, ice, sling and early motion", which is the lecture's treatment for AC separation types I-III (the notes: "I: Education, sling, analgesics, local therapy (ice) and early exercises · II: Same · III: Same").

  • A is reserved for types IV-V, the more displaced separations.
  • C is the surgical option for atraumatic, multidirectional glenohumeral instability, not an AC problem.
  • D is a surgical option for adhesive capsulitis.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: DG, a 40-year-old man. His X-rays (an AP view and a cross-table view) are shown. The case sits in the lecture's AC joint instability section.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.html: Education, ice, a sling and early exercises
Surgical repair of the AC joint

answer:
The correct answer is D. The follow-up image ("POST OP") shows his shoulder after operative fixation, and the lecture sends types IV-V AC separation to surgery. Separation is graded I to V by increasing displacement, so it is the size of the displacement on his films that sends him to the operating room.

  • A is the treatment for types I-III, the less displaced injuries.
  • B is the primary treatment for atraumatic, multidirectional glenohumeral instability, not for an AC separation.
  • C is a treatment for adhesive capsulitis, and AC joint injections are a local treatment for AC osteoarthritis, not for a displaced separation.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: 18 Yr M Hockey Player. His shoulder X-rays show an anterior shoulder (glenohumeral) dislocation.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.html: Reduction with analgesia, then recheck the nerves
Inferior capsular shift to tighten the capsule
Labral repair as the first treatment, before reduction
Sling, ice and early exercises without reduction

answer:
The correct answer is A. The X-ray shows an anterior shoulder dislocation, and the lecture follows that case with the reduction method: "Safety first! Monitors · Analgesia · Manipulation to correct deformity · Re-examine after: check neurovascular status", then a post-reduction X-ray. A traumatic dislocation is "torn loose", unidirectional, anterior >> posterior.

  • B is surgery for atraumatic multidirectional instability, and surgery there is uncommon.
  • C: labral repair is for young or recurrent dislocators - an option after the shoulder is reduced, not instead of reducing it.
  • D is the treatment for AC separation types I-III; a dislocated glenohumeral joint has to be reduced.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html:
Case: 47 Yr Old Male

  • 4-month history of Lt shoulder pain
  • Progressive loss of motion
  • Diabetic

His shoulder X-rays are shown.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is C. The case sits in the adhesive capsulitis talk, and the lecture gives the reasoning: the differential is arthritis and post-trauma deformity, "BUT... X-rays normal · No trauma". Adhesive capsulitis is a spontaneous, global restriction of active and passive motion with no known intrinsic shoulder disorder, seen in 20% of patients with diabetes, with onset in the 40s and 50s.

  • A: noninflammatory arthritis would show on the X-ray (asymmetric joint space, osteophytes, cysts, subchondral sclerosis). His X-rays are normal.
  • B: rotator cuff arthropathy shows the humerus migrated up against the acromion with arthritis (Muscles of the Shoulder lecture); his X-rays are normal.
  • D: there was no trauma.

options.html: Referral to orthopedics for surgical management
Conservative management with sling, ice, analgesia and early exercises

answer: The correct answer is B. The AC joint is essentially congruent (perhaps some mild upward migration). You will NOT be asked to distinguish between all types on X-rays, but should be familiar with what features would lead you to think the patient needs a surgery, largely significant dislocation or compromise.

stem: You are seeing a patient in your clinic who is complaining of generalized shoulder discomfort. She tells you that she has dislocated her shoulder at least a dozen times in her life and she feels like it's very unstable. Sometimes it just pops out on its own if she positions the arm in the wrong way. She'd like to prevent re-dislocation but has never tried any treatment. She also has a history of dislocating her other shoulder at least 3 times. What type of treatment pathway would you most likely recommend for her?
answer: The correct answer is A. In patients who have recurrent atraumatic dislocations and generalized joint laxity (as demonstrated by her history of dislocating both joints multiple times), the treatment of choice is usually non-surgical and focused on physiotherapy (strengthening the muscular/proprioceptive inputs to shoulder stability)

stem: Diagnosis? (verbatim; the case sets the two men side by side and asks once, banked here as one question per man)
answer:
The correct answer is B. The notes' answer labels Man #1 "Degenerative (Osteoarthritis)". Every row matches the degenerative pattern in the notes: pain with activity (stairs, running), gradual onset over months with no precipitant, episodic rather than constant, and the other knee going the same way.

  • A, C are the inflammatory arthritides the notes name; the inflammatory pattern is pain at rest, morning stiffness, swelling, warmth and redness, none of which he has.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Three Dropped Feet (aka dorsiflexion weakness). Foot #1: Inability to dorsiflex · Sudden onset · No sensory loss · Pain to palpation dorsum of foot, pain with resisted dorsiflexion testing · Sports injury

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is A. The case reveals tendon rupture. The weakness pattern table gives MSK weakness from a tear: usually painful, acute, no objective sensory abnormalities. Foot #1 is painful at the dorsum of the foot and on resisted dorsiflexion, with no sensory loss, after a sports injury.

  • B, C are nerve injuries, and both of the lecture's nerve feet have sensory loss in that nerve's or root's territory.
  • D the lumbosacral plexus is one of the sites the lecture's localization diagram shows along the path, but a plexus lesion is a nerve lesion and would bring sensory change too.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Three Dropped Feet (aka dorsiflexion weakness). Foot #2: Inability to dorsiflex · Sudden onset · Sensory loss lateral leg · No pain ankle/foot; sensitive to pressure at fibular head · Post-op laproscopic cholecystectomy

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is C. The case reveals common peroneal nerve injury. It is the lower motor neuron pattern in the lecture's weakness table: sensory abnormality confined to that nerve's territory (the lateral leg), with the tender spot over the fibular head, where the lecture's localization diagram puts the common peroneal nerve. Nothing hurts at the ankle or foot, and the story is a surgery, not an injury to the leg.

  • A a tendon rupture has no sensory loss and hurts at the tendon (Foot #1).
  • B an L5 root lesion brings back pain and numbness onto the dorsal foot as well (Foot #3).
  • D nothing in the history or exam localizes above the knee; the tenderness sits at the fibular head.

preamble.html: Three Dropped Feet (aka dorsiflexion weakness). Foot #3: Inability to dorsiflex · Sudden onset · Decreased sensation lateral leg and dorsal foot · Painful from back down to toes · Started after lifting and twisting with heavy boxy

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is B. The lecture reveals L5 radiculopathy (spinal root injury). The pain runs from the back down to the toes and the numbness covers the lateral leg and the dorsum of the foot, the L5 dermatome in the non-mechanical lecture's root table; lifting and twisting is the story of an acute disc herniation, which in the lumbar spine hits the root below (an L4/5 disc → L5).

  • A a tendon rupture has no sensory loss (Foot #1).
  • C a common peroneal lesion is numb on the lateral leg only, tender at the fibular head, with no back pain (Foot #2).
  • D the plexus sits below the root on the lecture's diagram; pain starting in the back after lifting localizes to the root.

stem: Match each deformity to the affected nerve.
answer:
The pairings:

DeformityAffected nerve
Waiter's tip hand / Erb-DuchenneUpper brachial plexus injury
Hand of benedictionMedian nerve
Wrist dropRadial nerve
Ulnar Claw / Klumpke's paralysisUlnar nerve

Waiter's tip hand: Upper brachial plexus injury (C5-C6) → Erb-Duchenne palsy, the "waiter's tip" posture.

Hand of benediction: median nerve — the hand of benediction (inability to flex the index and middle fingers when attempting to make a fist).

Wrist drop: radial nerve — the radial nerve supplies the extensor compartment (Q15), so its loss drops the wrist.

Ulnar claw: ulnar nerve — the ulnar claw.

From Anatomy of the Brachial Plexus. The claw is the ulnar nerve's signature, from loss of the intrinsic hand muscles, and the lecture puts the ulnar nerve on the medial cord carrying C8 and T1 only - the inferior trunk. That shared root is the link to Klumpke's palsy: a lower plexus injury (C8-T1, classically after shoulder dystocia) takes out the ulnar supply at its origin and produces the same claw.

  • The radial nerve (posterior cord, C5-T1) gives wrist drop, not a claw.
  • The median nerve (all five roots) gives thenar weakness, not the ulnar claw.
  • The upper plexus (Erb's palsy, C5-C6) spares the hand.

stem: Ms. S, a 25-year-old female, sees you in your family clinic for right arm pain that has been bothering her for 2 months. Which of the following symptoms would lead you to believe that she has neuropathic pain? (Choose 5 answers)
answer:
The correct answers are A, E, H, I, J. Symptoms of neuropathic pain:

  • Shooting pain ← A
  • Tingling/numbness ← E (also known as paresthesias)
  • Burning pain ← H
  • Hyperalgesia ← I — pain beyond expectation in response to a normally painful stimulus
  • Allodynia ← J — pain in response to a normally non-painful stimulus

Note that F (diminished sensation) and G (analgesia) are negative sensory phenomena — they can accompany nerve injury but are not the pain symptoms the question asks for. B and C are nociceptive descriptors (compare Q11).

stem: A 25-year-old female patient presents to the clinic with numbness and tingling in her right arm and hand. She reports that the symptoms are worse at night and interfere with her sleep. On examination, you note weakness in the muscles innervated by the median nerve, including the flexor pollicis longus, the flexor digitorum profundus, and the pronator teres. Which nerve is most likely affected in this patient?
answer:
The answer is C — the median nerve.

From Anatomy of the Neurovascular Supply of the Distal Upper Extremity. The stem names the nerve, so the thinking worth doing is about the level. The lecture gives the median nerve two compression sites: through pronator teres at the elbow (pronator syndrome) and under the flexor retinaculum at the wrist (carpal tunnel syndrome). Flexor pollicis longus, the lateral FDP and pronator teres are all supplied above the carpal tunnel, so their weakness places the lesion proximally - even though night-time paresthesia sounds like carpal tunnel.

  • A fails: the radial nerve supplies the extensors (wrist drop), none of the listed flexors.
  • B fails: the ulnar nerve supplies the medial FDP and the intrinsics (claw), not FPL or pronator teres.
  • D fails: the axillary nerve supplies deltoid and teres minor at the shoulder.

flags.title: No answer in the workbook, and the stem gives itself away
flags.html:
The key stops at Q83, so Q86 is unanswered. C is unambiguous only because the stem itself names the median nerve ("weakness in the muscles innervated by the median nerve") before asking which nerve is affected.

The clinically interesting point the question fails to ask: the muscles listed — flexor pollicis longus, flexor digitorum profundus and pronator teres — are proximal median-innervated muscles that lie above the carpal tunnel. Weakness in them therefore points to a proximal median neuropathy (pronator teres syndrome / anterior interosseous involvement), not carpal tunnel syndrome — even though the "worse at night, interferes with sleep" history is written to sound like carpal tunnel.

stem: Match each definition to the correct rotator cuff pathology.
answer:
The pairings:

DefinitionRotator cuff pathology
This pathology is indicated by tendon inflammation without evidence of structural defect.Stage I rotator cuff disease
This pathology is defined as rotator cuff arthropathy.Stage IV rotator cuff disease
This pathology is indicated by a partial thickness tear in the rotator cuff.Stage II rotator cuff disease
This pathology is indicated by a full thickness tear in the rotator cuff.Stage III rotator cuff disease

Stage I: inflammation with no structural defect is the earliest stage.

Stage IV: From Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Shoulder. Rotator cuff disease is progressive, and the notes' spectrum ends in rotator cuff arthropathy: a massive cuff defect lets the humeral head migrate superiorly until it touches the acromion, and arthritis follows. That end stage is Stage IV in the workbook's scheme, and it is the stage treated by shoulder arthroplasty rather than cuff repair.

Stage II: Stage II is the first structural defect: a partial-thickness defect of the supraspinatus tendon at its articular end (not the bursal end) - the "mild tear". It follows from the lecture's intrinsic mechanism: vascularity is lost from the articular portion of the tendon distally, so that is where fibres fail first. Cuff repair is reserved for Stage II-III disease that fails conservative care.

Stage III: a full-thickness supraspinatus defect - the "severe tear". With the cuff no longer holding the head down, the humerus displaces superiorly and synovial fluid can leak into the surrounding tissue (swelling). It is still short of the massive defect and arthritis that define arthropathy. Stage I, by contrast, is intact but inflamed (the impingement stage, the one acromioplasty treats).

The workbook also offered a Stage V; there is no Stage V, and it was never used.

See rotator cuff tendinopathy.

stem: A patient is complaining about pain in the posterior left thigh and imaging reveals a left paracentral disc herniation at L5/S1 level. Which nerve root is most likely affected?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

From the spinal disc herniation note linked from 02.2 - Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain. A paracentral lumbar herniation (the most common kind) compresses the nerve of the lower vertebra, so L5/S1 hits S1. Only a far lateral herniation catches the upper root.

  • A fails: L4 would need an L3/L4 paracentral or an L4/L5 far-lateral herniation.
  • B fails: L5 is the upper root at this level, hit only if the disc were far lateral.
  • D fails: S2 is a level below the traversing root.

Posterior-thigh pain fits an S1 radiculopathy; 03.2 would confirm it with a lateral-foot sensory change, weak plantar flexion and a reduced Achilles reflex.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a typically radiographical finding for degenerative shoulder arthritis?
answer: The correct answer is D. Erosions are typically found in inflammatory arthritis. Asymmetric joint space narrowing, osteophytes, cycs and subchondral sclerosis are the typical radiological findings for degenerative (non-inflammatory) arthritis.

stem: A patient comes into your office after falling on their elbow while playing sports, now complaining about numbness and tingling with their pinky. What spinal roots is the affected nerve originated from?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

From 01 - Anatomy of the Brachial Plexus. A blow to the elbow with numbness in the little finger is the ulnar nerve at the "funny bone", behind the medial epicondyle. The ulnar nerve comes off the medial cord, so it carries only C8 and T1 (the inferior trunk).

  • A (C5-T1) is the whole plexus, and the roots of the median and radial nerves, not the ulnar.
  • B (C5-C7) is the lateral-cord pattern (e.g., musculocutaneous), which spares the little finger.
  • D (C7) is a single root whose dermatome is the middle finger, not the fifth.

stem: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding elbow dislocation?

options.html: Anterior dislocation is more common than posterior dislocation
The most common mechanism of the injury is falling onto outstretched hand
Ulnar nerve is most of concern during a typical elbow dislocation
One of the complications to watch for is the compartment syndrome of the forearm

answer:
The correct answer is A. Posterior dislocaions are the most common.

From 05.2 - Clinical Approach to the Elbow. The embedded elbow dislocation note says posterior dislocation is most common, so the statement that anterior is more common is the false one.

  • B is true: the typical mechanism is a FOOSH (or bracing in a car crash).
  • C is true: of the nerves, the ulnar nerve is the one the note singles out, as it runs right behind the medial epicondyle.
  • D is true: compartment syndrome is listed with capsule rupture, ligament tears and broken skin, which is why the note calls it an emergency.

Lateral epicondylitis can produce pain with passive stretch of wrist extension
Medial epicondylitis can produce pain with resisted wrist extension

stem: During your ER rotation, a patient is brought to the ER complaining of a sudden loss of sensation in the buttocks area. They’ve been experiencing bilateral leg and back pain for the past 24 hours. What is the best next step?

options.html: Reassure that the patient that this is mechanical back pain and prescribe NSAIDs.

answer:
The correct answer is C. An MRI is needed to rule out cauda equina syndrome

From 02.2 - Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain. New saddle anesthesia on a background of bilateral leg and back pain is a neurologic red flag, and red flags are the one situation where back pain gets imaged. The picture is cauda equina syndrome (the notes list it among the spine problems to recognize; 03.2 adds MRI when there is significant neurologic compromise), a surgical emergency where decompression is time-critical.

  • A fails: mechanical back pain is a diagnosis made only once red flags are absent.
  • B fails: physiotherapy is conservative care, which red flags override.
  • D fails because C is right.

stem: A 47-year-old painter has had shoulder pain with overhead work for a year despite education, NSAIDs and physiotherapy. MRI shows an inflamed but structurally intact rotator cuff (stage I). Which procedure fits this stage?
answer: The correct answer is E. Rotator cuff disease: stage I intact but inflamed, stage II partial-thickness defect, stage III full-thickness defect with the humeral head migrating up, and cuff arthropathy when the head abuts the acromion. Surgery (for ongoing pain, weakness or acute injury) is subacromial decompression for stage I, cuff repair for II-III, and arthroplasty for arthropathy.

answer: The correct answer is B. Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow (cubital tunnel) comes from leaning on the elbow, direct trauma, prolonged flexion during sleep, or nerve subluxation. stem: A 20-year-old man falls onto his outstretched hand. He has swelling and tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. Wrist and scaphoid x-rays are normal. What is the most appropriate management?

options.html: Reassure him that it is a sprain
Immobilize and arrange CT or MRI

answer: The correct answer is C. The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone and x-rays can look normal. Its blood supply is retrograde, so a missed fracture risks non-union and osteonecrosis. If FOOSH plus swelling and tenderness, treat it as fractured and follow up with CT or MRI.

stem: A distal radius fracture: on the lateral X-ray the joint surface is tilted 20° dorsally (a normal wrist has about 12° of palmar tilt). What is the next step in management?

options.html: Cast in the position found, then rehabilitate

answer: The correct answer is B. The lecture follows this fracture from "Is it Crooked? 20 deg DF" through adequate analgesia (hematoma block, regional anaesthesia or conscious sedation), traction and closed reduction to an acceptable result. Its treatment principles put closed reduction second, after age, and surgical reduction only if reduction is inadequate, so open fixation is not the first step. Casting it as it lies leaves it crooked, which alters distal radio-ulnar joint motion and restricts forearm rotation. Fusion is the treatment for radiocarpal arthritis from a joint surface left uneven, not for a fresh fracture. (Reasoning written from the lecture's sequence; the lecture itself poses no question.)

stem: A distal radius fracture that enters the joint has been treated by closed reduction, but the X-ray still shows a step in the joint surface. What is the next step in management?

options.html: Recast it with a tighter three-point mould and recheck
Accept the step and begin rehabilitation
Open reduction internal fixation or external fixation
Wrist fusion now, to prevent arthritis

answer: The correct answer is C. After "Still not smooth" the lecture goes to open reduction internal fixation or external fixation, and its summary says "if reduction is inadequate: surgical reduction". A step of more than 1 mm is associated with post-traumatic arthrosis, so accepting it is wrong. A tighter cast cannot reduce the joint surface, and "well molded doesn't mean TIGHT". Fusion treats the radiocarpal arthritis that follows an uneven joint; it is not used to prevent it. (Reasoning written from the lecture's sequence.)

stem: CASE 2: a 25-year-old man. His PA and lateral wrist X-rays and a CT of the wrist are shown; the CT shows an undisplaced fracture line through the scaphoid. What management does the lecture show for him?

options.html: Operative fixation through a volar approach
Closed reduction under a hematoma block
Wrist fusion to prevent late arthrosis

answer: The correct answer is D. The lecture follows the case with "Features of a Good Cast" and "8 Weeks Post Injury: Casted - CT Scan: Healed fracture", matching its rule: undisplaced or distal → cast until union; displaced or proximal → surgery. Operative fixation through a volar approach is for the displaced proximal pole fracture of Case 3. Closed reduction under a hematoma block is the distal radius technique and has nothing to reduce in an undisplaced fracture. Fusion is not a treatment for a fresh scaphoid fracture; late arthrosis is a complication. The case also shows the lecture's "be SUSPICIOUS" point: the fracture was confirmed on CT. preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 45-year-old woman, a construction worker who smokes half a pack a day, has had 2 weeks of acute, severe, sharp low back pain (R>L) that began lifting a heavy box. It is worse with walking and with standing after prolonged sitting, slightly better with naproxen, and radiates down the right leg to the shin. On the red flag screen she reports only tingling down the right lateral leg and dorsal foot. She stands slightly forward flexed, is diffusely tender over the right lumbar region, resists forward flexion and extension because of pain, and has mild weakness of right ankle dorsiflexion and toe extension.

stem: Which nerve root is most likely affected?
answer:
The correct answer is C. The session concludes L5 radiculopathy, presumably from degenerative disc disease (spondylosis). Tingling over the lateral leg and dorsal foot is the L5 sensory territory, and dorsiflexion and toe extension are L5 muscles in the root table; pain shooting down one leg with a neurological deficit is a problem to the side (a root), not the centre.

  • A L3 supplies hip flexion, knee extension and hip adduction, with sensation at the medial knee; none of these is affected.
  • B L4 gives the patellar reflex, knee extension and the medial malleolus; it shares dorsiflexion, but not toe extension or the dorsal foot.
  • D S1 gives plantar flexion, the ankle reflex and the lateral heel; her weakness is in dorsiflexion and toe extension.

It is worse with walking and with standing after prolonged sitting, slightly better with naproxen, and radiates down the right leg to the shin. On the red flag screen she reports only tingling down the right lateral leg and dorsal foot. She stands slightly forward flexed, is diffusely tender over the right lumbar region, resists forward flexion and extension because of pain, and has mild weakness of right ankle dorsiflexion and toe extension.

stem: Assuming a paracentral disc herniation, at which disc level is it most likely?
answer:
The correct answer is C. A lumbar disc herniation affects the nerve of the lower vertebra: an L4/5 herniation affects L5. Lumbar roots exit below their vertebra, and because of the angle they travel, the L4 root has already left by the L4/5 disc, so a paracentral disc catches the traversing L5 root.

  • A An L2/3 disc would catch the traversing L3 root.
  • B An L3/4 disc would catch L4, the root that gives the patellar reflex and the medial malleolus.
  • D An L5/S1 disc would catch S1: plantar flexion, the ankle reflex, the lateral heel.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 45-year-old woman, a construction worker who smokes half a pack a day, has had 2 weeks of acute, severe, sharp low back pain (R>L) that began lifting a heavy box. It is worse with walking and with standing after prolonged sitting, slightly better with naproxen, and radiates down the right leg to the shin. On the red flag screen she reports only tingling down the right lateral leg and dorsal foot. She stands slightly forward flexed, is diffusely tender over the right lumbar region, resists forward flexion and extension because of pain, and has mild weakness of right ankle dorsiflexion and toe extension.

stem: She has no red flags. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.html: Lumbar MRI before any treatment begins
Stay active, physiotherapy and an NSAID
A week of bed rest and a short opioid course
Referral to spine surgery for discectomy

answer:
The correct answer is B. The session's plan: education (most improve spontaneously over 6 months; know the red flags that should bring her back; keep moving, no bed rest), then non-pharmacologic care (relative rest from aggravating activities, physiotherapy), then pharmacologic care (acetaminophen, NSAIDs, neuropathic pain agents). The same plan applies to radiculopathy without red flags.

  • A With no red flags and pain under 6 weeks, low back pain needs no imaging (Choosing Wisely Canada); imaging rarely changes management.
  • C Bed rest is the opposite of the advice; opioids are at most a short course for severe radicular pain, which she does not have.
  • D Surgery is for refractory, leg-dominant pain or progressive neurological symptoms, after conservative care.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The woman above improved after about 7 months and felt fine until yesterday, when her back "went out" standing from a chair. Since then the pain is severe and radiates down both legs to the toes with paraesthesiae. This morning she has trouble walking, urinary dribbling and cannot feel the toilet paper when she wipes. No fever, constitutional symptoms, trauma, night pain or morning stiffness. She needs help onto the table; knee extension is 4/5 and dorsiflexion and toe extension 3/5 bilaterally. Digital rectal exam: limited voluntary contraction. She is asking for pain medication and an antibiotic for a urinary tract infection.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Cauda equina syndrome with acute onset. She has the neurological red flags for the lower back: bilateral progressive weakness, saddle anaesthesia (cannot feel the toilet paper), urinary dysfunction (dribbling, i.e. overflow from retention) and reduced anal tone on rectal exam. A central disc compressing the whole cauda equina is a problem to the centre.

  • A A root lesion is one-sided and spares the bladder and saddle; her deficit is bilateral with sphincter involvement.
  • C Stenosis causes neurogenic claudication eased by bending forward, with no bladder change, and develops over months, not overnight.
  • D The dribbling is from loss of bladder control, not infection: there is no dysuria, and the saddle anaesthesia and weakness are neurological.

Digital rectal exam: limited voluntary contraction. She is asking for pain medication and an antibiotic for a urinary tract infection.

stem: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.html: A urine culture and an antibiotic for UTI
Send to the ER now and call spine surgery
An outpatient lumbar MRI within six weeks
An oral opioid and review in one week

answer:
The correct answer is B. This is an emergency. Leg weakness and urinary incontinence began this morning: don't wait. Send her straight to the emergency department, calling ahead to describe the case and request spine surgery involvement. Cauda equina syndrome needs an urgent MRI and decompression, ideally within 48 hours.

  • A Treating the bladder symptoms as an infection misses the compression causing them.
  • C Suspected cauda equina is a red-flag indication for an urgent MRI, not an outpatient one.
  • D Analgesia alone delays decompression while the deficit progresses.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 61-year-old man, a financial advisor with hypertension who smokes about 5 cigarettes a day, has 6 months of insidious, deep, aching low back pain (L>R) with no radiation, worse with prolonged walking and with bending or twisting, and no numbness, tingling or weakness. Exam: no abnormality on inspection, focal tenderness, reduced flexion, extension and left lateral flexion, normal lower-limb strength and sensation. A clinic X-ray months ago led to Percocet, which helped. On direct questioning he reports blood in his urine on and off for 4 months and significant night sweats, with no fever, weight loss, inflammatory features or trauma.

stem: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.html: Reassure and reassess in six weeks

answer:
The correct answer is A. Hematuria for 4 months and night sweats are red flags: a visceral source (associated GU symptoms) and a possible neoplasm (night sweats). Red flags call for targeted tests, so the session works him up with a urinalysis and a renal ultrasound.

  • B An X-ray screens alignment and fractures; it cannot explain the hematuria.
  • C Conservative care is for back pain without red flags, and he has two.
  • D Watchful waiting is also for pain without red flags; his hematuria needs investigating now.

Ultrasound finds no stones but a solitary mass on the left kidney.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is A. Urgent urology consultation diagnosed renal cell carcinoma. A solitary renal mass with hematuria and night sweats is a visceral and neoplastic cause of back pain, the kind the red flag screen exists to find. ⭐ Ask about red flags even when an earlier clinic has already labelled the pain and it responds to analgesia.

  • B The ultrasound rules out stones.
  • C Facet pain is mechanical and would not explain hematuria or a renal mass.
  • D Stenosis causes neurogenic claudication with leg symptoms; he has no radiation or neurological change.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 73-year-old retired accountant with hypertension, diabetes and bilateral hip replacements for osteoarthritis has long-standing neck pain, worse over 2-3 weeks: a constant dull ache with sharp pangs, sore heavy shoulders, pain down both arms, worse with neck movement in any direction. For 2 weeks he has felt "off", with poor appetite, fatigue and some flushing. For 2 months his hands have been numb and tingling; his arms feel weak; he has noticed urinary incontinence and feels "drunk" when walking. Exam: stands forward flexed with a wide-based, unsteady gait, limited neck range of motion, arms ~4/5, hands feel "weird". Reflexes: reduced at biceps and brachioradialis, normal triceps, increased at knees and ankles; mildly increased right plantar flexor tone with an upgoing right toe.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Cervical myelopathy: compression of the cervical cord, of any cause, a serious problem to the centre. Below the level he has the cord signs: loss of hand dexterity (numb, weird hands), urinary incontinence and gait and balance change (wide-based, "drunk"), with hyperreflexia, increased tone and an upgoing toe in the legs.

  • A The reduced biceps and brachioradialis reflexes do point to C5-C6 roots, but roots cannot explain the brisk leg reflexes, upgoing toe, incontinence or ataxic gait.
  • C Mechanical neck pain has no neurological signs, and his malaise and flushing are red flags.
  • D Shoulder tendinopathy causes pain with movement and no neurological change.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 73-year-old retired accountant with hypertension, diabetes and bilateral hip replacements for osteoarthritis has long-standing neck pain, worse over 2-3 weeks: a constant dull ache with sharp pangs, sore heavy shoulders, pain down both arms, worse with neck movement in any direction. For 2 weeks he has felt "off", with poor appetite, fatigue and some flushing. For 2 months his hands have been numb and tingling; his arms feel weak; he has noticed urinary incontinence and feels "drunk" when walking. Exam: stands forward flexed with a wide-based, unsteady gait, limited neck range of motion, arms ~4/5, hands feel "weird". Reflexes: reduced at biceps and brachioradialis, normal triceps, increased at knees and ankles; mildly increased right plantar flexor tone with an upgoing right toe.

stem: What does the combination of reduced biceps and brachioradialis reflexes with brisk knee and ankle reflexes indicate?

options.html: Root signs at the lesion, cord signs below
A peripheral neuropathy affecting all four limbs
Bilateral L5 radiculopathy from lumbar stenosis
A primary muscle disease of the shoulder girdle

answer:
The correct answer is A. In cervical myelopathy the roots at the level of the compression can be compromised, so it presents like a radiculopathy at that level (here C5-C6: reduced biceps and brachioradialis), while the cord is compromised too, so it presents like a spinal cord injury below the lesion (upper motor neuron signs: hyperreflexia, spasticity, upgoing toe).

  • B A neuropathy lowers reflexes everywhere; it does not make the legs brisk.
  • C A lumbar root lesion lowers leg reflexes, and cannot explain arm findings.
  • D Muscle disease does not produce hyperreflexia, an upgoing toe or sensory change.

answer:
From Anatomy of the Brachial Plexus. Reasoned answer (mine, not the workbook's): A, tentatively. The notes' brachial plexus notes name the two classic patterns - upper (Erb's palsy, C5-C6) and lower (Klumpke's palsy, C8-T1), both after shoulder dystocia - but never say which is commoner. In general the upper-trunk injury is the commoner pattern (traction that widens the neck-shoulder angle), and its territory is the deltoid and biceps: the axillary nerve and the musculocutaneous nerve. Of those, A is the more defensible, and E is nearly as good.

  • B, C each draw on all five roots (Anatomy of the Brachial Plexus), so a partial plexus injury rarely silences either completely.
  • D is the lower-plexus nerve (C8-T1): the less common pattern, even though it is the likely "intended" answer after Q61.

Not a letter to memorise - the question has no single defensible answer as written (see the flag on this question).

flags.html: This year's lectures do not teach this. Checked against Anatomy of the Brachial Plexus, the nearest lecture, which does not mention it.

flags.title: No answer in the workbook — and the question is ambiguous
flags.html:
The key stops at Q83, so Q85 is unanswered, and unlike Q84 there is no other passage in the workbook that settles it.

The likely intended answer is D, the ulnar nerve, on the reasoning that the lower plexus (C8-T1) is the ulnar nerve's origin and lower-plexus/Klumpke-type injuries are what Q61 has just covered. However, brachial plexus injury patterns depend entirely on mechanism — upper plexus (Erb-Duchenne, Q61) injuries are the more common obstetric and traction pattern, which would favour the axillary or musculocutaneous nerve — so the "most commonly affected" framing has no single defensible answer as written. Verify against a real source; do not memorize a letter here.

stem: A patient comes to you following a soccer game where a soccer ball was kicked up striking the end of their index finger head on. On examination the finger is swollen and they have lost the ability to keep the DIP in an extended position. Function of the rest of the finger, while hindered by swelling, appears to be normal. What is this injury called and how do you manage it?

options.html: Boutonnière deformity and it is managed with surgery
Mallet finger and it is managed with radiologic imaging and splinting in an extended position
Jersey finger and it is managed with radiologic imaging, grip and finger extension exercises
Trigger finger and it is a self-limiting condition

answer:
The correct answer is B. mallet finger — loss of DIP extension after a direct blow to the fingertip. Management is continuous extension for 6-8 weeks. Surgery has been used but is often not necessary; it becomes an option for patients whose injury becomes chronic and fails splinting.

Contrast the named deformities: Boutonnière is loss of PIP extension; Jersey finger is loss of DIP flexion (FDP avulsion); trigger finger is catching on flexion (see Q38).

stem: A 55-year-old man comes to you with complaints of his 3rd and 4th digits clicking when he flexes and extends his fingers. He is currently limiting his flexion in order to avoid reaching the point where the clicking occurs because he has had incidents where his fingers lock and it is very painful to unlock them. This has resulted in him not being able to manage his duties at work as a manual labourer. What is the most appropriate management?

options.html: Splint in extension for two weeks
Inject steroids into the area to try and relieve pain/swelling

answer:
The correct answer is C. This is trigger finger, and the question is really about where on the escalation ladder this patient sits:

  • B (nothing) is reasonable when it is not painful, the patient is not pushing for therapy, and function is unaffected — but his work is affected.
  • C (steroid injection) is reasonable because he wants further treatment and his function is impaired.
  • D (surgery) — surgical release of the flexor tendon sheath — is for patients who have failed a trial of steroid injection and remain impaired.

Subtrochanteric – endangering the profunda femoris artery

answer: The correct answer is C. A femoral neck fracture endangers the circumflex arteries, which supply the majority of perfusion to the femoral head — hence the risk of avascular necrosis. See osteonecrosis of the hip.

options.html: Upper Right Quadrant – to avoid the sciatic nerve
Lower Right Quadrant - to avoid the piriformis
Lower Left Quadrant – to avoid the femoral artery and vein
Upper Left Quadrant – to avoid the sciatic nerve

answer: The workbook's answer is A, to avoid the sciatic nerve. Injecting in this quadrant is least likely to damage the sciatic nerve along its course in the posterior thigh.

flags.title: Badly constructed question
flags.html: Options A and D are functionally identical — both name a superior quadrant and both give the same reason (avoiding the sciatic nerve), and the stem never establishes whether "right/left" means lateral/medial or the patient's right/left buttock. The teaching point being aimed at is the upper outer (superolateral) quadrant, which is the standard safe site. stem: Where would you most commonly find a femoral hernia among the contents of the femoral canal (structures listed are lateral to medial)?

options.html: Lymph nodes, hernia, vein, artery, nerve
Nerve, artery, vein, hernia, lymph nodes
Nerve, hernia, artery, vein, empty space, lymph nodes
Lymph nodes, hernia, artery, vein, empty space

answer:
The correct answer is B. Lateral to medial: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space, Lymph nodes — the acronym NAVEL.

The hernia occupies the easiest route available, which is the Empty space — so B is right because it places the hernia exactly where the "E" of NAVEL sits.

stem: A patient has pain during walking in their weight bearing leg. The pain is localized to the anterior groin region, as the leg goes into extension. You place the patient in a supine position and examine their muscular function and range of motion. Your findings are relatively normal except pain on hip flexion and passive hip extension near the end range of motion. Which of the following statements are true?

options.html: The most likely muscle group involved are the hamstrings
This is referred to as a Trendelenburg gait and is a result of gluteus medius injury/weakness
This is likely referred pain from sciatic nerve impingement
This could be a result of muscle, tendon sheath, or bursitis pain associated with the iliopsoas muscle

answer:
The correct answer is D. The iliopsoas and its associated structures are the likely cause, because both active recruitment (hip flexion) and passive stretching (hip extension) of the psoas reproduce the pain — that pattern is the diagnosis.

A and C are wrong on location: that pain would be in the posterior buttock and down the thigh, not the anterior groin. B is wrong on gait: a Trendelenburg pattern with pelvic instability is not what the case describes.

stem: Which muscle group and innervation is not correctly matched:

options.html: Quadriceps muscles supplied by the femoral nerve
Adductor longus, brevis and magnus supplied by the obturator nerve, except the hamstring portion of magnus which is the tibial portion of the sciatic nerve
Gluteus maximus supplied by the superior gluteal nerve and the gluteus medius and minimus supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve

Semitendinosus, semimembranosus and the long head of the biceps femoris supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic and the short head of the biceps femoris supplied by the fibular division of the sciatic

answer:
The correct answer is C — it has the two gluteal nerves swapped. Gluteus maximus is supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve; gluteus medius and minimus by the superior gluteal nerve.

How to remember it: picture the muscles in anatomical position — medius and minimus are the more superior muscles, and conveniently they take the superior gluteal nerve. See femoral nerve, obturator nerve, sciatic nerve.

stem: A patient comes to you with persistent left hip pain that localizes to the side of the hip. They complain a lot of pain that has disturbed their sleep because they can no longer sleep on their left side. You perform a neurological examination and find no neurological findings. The patient is also found to be otherwise healthy without fever, weight loss or night sweats. What option is not suggested in the management of this patient?

options.html: Educate the patient about their condition

answer:
The correct answer is B. The patient has no red flags — note carefully that the sleep disturbance is caused by a change in position, not by night pain as such, and this presents as a likely trochanteric bursitis.

With no red flags, appropriate management is patient education about how to help themselves, physiotherapy, and analgesics to allow participation in therapy. MRI is not indicated.

stem: Identify the ligament that is incorrectly matched to its function in stabilizing the knee.

options.html: Medial collateral ligament – resist valgus force on the knee
Fibular collateral ligament – resist varus forces on the knee
Anterior cruciate ligament – resist posterior translation of the femur on the tibial plateau
Posterior cruciate ligament – resist anterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur

answer:
The correct answer is D. The PCL does not resist anterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur — that is the ACL's job.

Reason it from the exam manoeuvre: think of the posterior sag sign or the translation of the tibia during the posterior drawer test (which tests for PCL rupture), and you can see the PCL resists POSTERIOR translation of the tibia relative to the femur. See anterior cruciate ligament.

stem: A rugby player plants his foot forward before being wrapped up and tackled from the right. The result is a valgus force on the knee in a flexed position with some external rotation of the lower leg. What structures are commonly injured in this type of trauma?

options.html: The fibular collateral ligament and the lateral meniscus
The quadriceps tendon and the IT band
The anterior cruciate ligament, medial meniscus and the Medial collateral ligament
The medial meniscus, posterior cruciate ligament, the hamstrings muscles

answer:
The correct answer is C. This is the Unhappy Triad: ACL + medial meniscus + MCL. Trace the mechanism:

  • The valgus force overcomes the MCL → MCL injury
  • Because the MCL attaches to the medial meniscus, an MCL tear of this nature drags a medial meniscal tear with it
  • The ACL is injured by the combination of external rotation of the tibia while the knee is semi-flexed

The key's own comment: "This is guaranteed to be on your test."

stem: Which of the following regarding meniscal injury is true?

options.html: Lateral meniscal tears should be suspected with injury of the fibular collateral ligament because it is fused to the lateral meniscus
Tears of the more central meniscus are faster to heal because they receive blood supply from the geniculate vessels
The peripheral portion of the meniscus receives better blood supply from the capsular vessels than the central portion
The lateral meniscus is often involved in what is referred to as the unhappy triad

answer:
The correct answer is C. The peripheral meniscus is better supplied by the capsular vessels — which is why peripheral tears heal the quickest.

  • B is backwards: central tears are nourished only by synovial fluid and are relatively slow to heal.
  • D is the wrong meniscus: it is the medial meniscus that features in the unhappy triad (Q26).
  • A is the wrong pair: the fibular collateral ligament and lateral meniscus are not connected — it is the medial pair (MCL and medial meniscus) that are fused.

See meniscus tear.

stem: A 25-year-old patient comes to your office complaining of pain on the lateral side of the knee. There is no history of trauma. He experiences it most during workouts such as squatting and lunges and when climbing the stairs to his apartment. On examination you find he has normal flexion and extension with no neurological findings. On palpation you find tenderness over the lateral side of the knee and fibular head. The knee is stable during the anterior/posterior drawer test as well as during varus and valgus stress. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is E. iliotibial band inflammation — a young active patient with characteristic pain over the IT band insertion during loading such as squatting and stair climbing.

  • A — no anterior knee swelling or pain reported
  • B — no signs of patellar pathology, and the pain is not anterior (see patellofemoral pain syndrome)
  • C and D — no history of trauma, which you would expect for these injuries in a young person, and no instability (MCL) or catching/locking (meniscal)

stem: A patient presents to clinic with loss of sensation over palmar aspect of digit 2 and 3 of right hand. The patient has a history of repetitive strain work as a factory worker and has a positive tunnel sign upon percussion of carpal tunnel. This leads you to suspect median nerve neuropathy. However, you are a smart medical student and know that a C6 radiculopathy is also on the differential for this patient. Which of the following clinical findings, if present, would be more consistent with a C6 radiculopathy and causes you to question your initial diagnosis of median nerve neuropathy.

options.html: The patient reports that the area of sensory loss over the palmar aspect of digit 2 and 3 is well defined
Weakness of biceps flexion and wrist extension
Wasting of thenar muscles and inability to oppose thumb
Loss of dexterity of 2nd and 3rd digit

answer: The correct answer is B. Biceps and wrist flexion are part of the C6 myotome which would be impaired if there was injury at the C6 nerve root as would be caused by a radiculopathy. All the rest are findings that would be consistent with a median nerve neuropathy at the wrist (more suggestive here due to positive tinel sign at the carpal tunnel area).

stem: Which of the following statements with regards to neurons and nerve injuries is true?

options.html: Endoneurium is the innermost layer of connective tissue within a nerve and it directly surrounds each axon
Peripheral nerves consist of a single axon wrapped in three layers of connective tissue, which are (from outer to inner most), epineurium, perineurium, and endoneurium.
Neurotmesis nerve injuries have the ability for spontaneous recovery because the epineurium is still intact, which serves as a path for regenerating fibers to grow along
Myelin injuries take a relatively longer time to recover than axonal injuries, possessing a recovery rate of 1 inch per month (1mm/day)

answer: The correct answer is A. B is false, there are many axons contained in a single nerve. C is false, neurotmesis injuries do not have the ability to spontaneously recover because the epineurium is not intact. D is false, axonal injuries are slower with a rate of 1inch/month.

stem: Which of the following pathologies is it NOT possible for electrodiagnostic studies (EDX) (included EMG and NCS studies) to detect?
answer: The correct answer is D. It is not possible for EDX studies to detect CNS pathology like stroke or multiple sclerosis. All the others are possible. NCS can be used to to assess health of myelin sheath and axon while EMG can be used to measure muscle functions in isolation.

stem: A patient is to undergo coronary bypass surgery and needs a graft from another blood vessel from another site in the body to complete the procedure. You select to the Great Saphenous Vein to be the graft. What nerve are you likely to damage when you go to harvest this graft and what would the sensory neurological deficits be?

options.html: Saphenous nerve: loss of sensation along the medial thigh
Saphenous nerve: loss of sensation over medial knee, leg, and foot
Obturator nerve: loss of sensation over medial thigh
Obturator nerve: loss of sensation over medial knee, leg, and foot

answer: The correct answer is B. Saphenous nerve runs in close proximity to great saphenous vein and supplies the anteromedial aspect of the knee, leg, and foot. Obturator nerve runs deep in the medial compartment of the thigh and is unlikely to be damaged during this procedure, as the great saphenous vein is a superficial vein.

stem: A 76 year old female patient with osteoporosis presents to the ER in immense pain over her right hip around the region of the greater trochanter for the past 6hrs. She reports rolling off her couch when she was napping and landing on her hip. You order an xray and confirm a intrascapular femoral neck fracture. What is the next step in the management of this patient?

options.html: Recommend conservative management for this patient – non-weight bearing for 3-4 weeks
Urgent open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) within 48hrs
Urgent hemiarthroplasty or total hip arthroplasty within 48hrs

answer: The correct answer is D. With hip fractures, surgery outcomes are best when surgery is performed within 24-48hrs of the fracture. For older patients (60+), the surgical method of choice is a hemiarthroplasty or total hip arthroplasty over ORIF.

stem: Jon Hamilton, a 19-year-old man comes to the ER because of right wrist pain and swelling 2 hours after falling on an outstretched hand while skateboarding trying to impress his Ram Ranch™ roommates Aaron and Devin. His right wrist is swollen and tender; range of motion is limited by pain. There is tenderness to palpation in the area between the tendons of the abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis, and extensor pollicis longus muscle. His thumb can be opposed actively toward the other fingers. Muscle strength of the right hand is decreased. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is D. Scaphoid fractures typically occur following a fall on an outstretched hand. If pain occurs in the anatomical snuffbox (area between the tendons of the abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis, and extensor pollicis longus muscle) after trauma, the injury should be treated as a scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise to prevent possible complications such as avascular necrosis and bone nonunion.

stem: A 28-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 24 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a prenatal visit. She reports dull aching pain and paresthesia over her left hand for the last few weeks. The pain radiates to her shoulder and is worse at night. Her hand feels numb upon waking up in the morning. She has a sister who has multiple sclerosis. Her current medications include iron supplements and a multivitamin. Vital signs are within normal limits. When the wrist is passively held in full flexion, aggravation of paresthesia is perceived immediately. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's symptoms?

options.html: Lower trunk palsy of the brachial plexus

answer: The correct answer is C. Median nerve compression would be the cause of her symptoms given the clinical picture of carpal tunnel syndrome.

stem: While being arrested by London's finest for public indecency after a night at Jack’s. James Bunker's arms were handcuffed behind his back. What actions did his upper limb have to perform to get to this position? Write your answer here:
answer:
Shoulder aBduction, extension, Internal rotation, and Elbow flexion.

Break the position down joint by joint. The elbows are bent, so elbow flexion. The humerus swings behind the trunk, which is shoulder extension. The forearms turn inward so the hands meet at the small of the back, which is internal (medial) rotation. Bringing the two wrists together behind the body draws the arms toward the midline, which is adduction, not abduction. The muscle notes put this exact combination in one muscle: latissimus dorsi (from 02.1 - Anatomy of the Back & Neck) "extends, aDDucts and medially rotates the humerus". That is the hand-behind-the-back movement, and why the lats and teres major are what the cuffs load.

flags.html: The key lists shoulder aBduction. Reaching behind the back to bring the hands together is adduction with extension and internal rotation, the actions the latissimus dorsi and teres major notes give. Extension, internal rotation and elbow flexion in the key are right; read the abduction as an error.

stem: A 50-year-old woman has numbness of the thumb and index finger. Which finding most favours C6 radiculopathy over carpal tunnel syndrome?

options.html: Symptoms that wake her at night
Weakness of thumb abduction and opposition
Numbness extending up the lateral forearm

answer: The correct answer is E. In carpal tunnel syndrome, median nerve function proximal to the wrist is normal, so sensory change stays in the hand; symptoms are nocturnal and worse with wrist flexion or extension, with Tinel/Phalen positive and possible thumb (LOAF) weakness. C6 radiculopathy extends to the lateral forearm and weakens the wrist extensors. EMG/NCS distinguishes the two.

stem: A 65 year-old male presents to your clinic with a 2-year history of intermittent hip pain which localizes to the groin. He has not tried any specific therapy to date. After taking a careful history and doing a thorough physical examination, you determine the most likely diagnosis is osteoarthritis of the hip. The patient asks if he should have an MRI to confirm the diagnosis. What should you tell him?

options.html: Of course! MRI is the best test for arthritis!
Well… we should do an x-ray and CT scan instead, because they’re better at looking at bones!
Let’s start with an x-ray, it’s great at looking at bones and will help confirm my diagnosis!
Instead of an MRI, we should get an US! It’s faster to get so you won’t have to wait as long!

answer: The correct answer is C. "Let's start with an x-ray, it's great at looking at bones and will help confirm my diagnosis!" MRI is not required to confirm the diagnosis of arthritis; it comes with a lengthy waitlist and adds no benefit in confirming the diagnosis. X-ray and CT are better at looking at bones, but CT carries much more radiation, and arthritis can be confidently confirmed on X-ray. Ultrasound is a poor modality for assessing arthritis, especially in a deep joint like the hip.

stem: You are seeing a 71 year-old female with lateral hip pain. You can’t seem to decide whether the history is more in keeping with GTPS or hip OA. The patient then tells you she has absolutely no difficulties getting her socks on in the morning when she’s sitting down. Which one seems more likely now?
answer: The correct answer is A. GTPS (greater trochanteric pain syndrome). Putting socks on in a seated position needs hip flexion and external rotation (basically the FABER test), so it is commonly uncomfortable with hip osteoarthritis. People with GTPS normally have a relatively pain-free hip range of motion, so socks are not a problem, unless they are standing: a single-leg stance needs the hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus) to stay upright, those usually have some tendinopathy in GTPS, and using them hurts.

stem: A 19-year-old soccer player plants her foot and pivots, feels a pop, and her knee swells markedly within a few hours. Which examination manoeuvre is most accurate for the likely injury?
answer: The correct answer is D. Non-contact pivoting during deceleration with a pop and rapid hemarthrosis is classic for an ACL tear (a vessel runs through the ligament). The Lachman test has the best sensitivity and specificity; anterior drawer is weaker and pivot shift is mostly done in the OR. X-ray rules out fracture; MRI if the exam is unclear.

stem: A 30-year-old driver hits his flexed knee on the dashboard in a collision. He has poorly defined knee pain and minimal swelling. With both knees flexed, the affected tibia sags posteriorly. Which structure is most likely injured?
answer: The correct answer is E. PCL injury follows a direct blow to the anterior tibia with the knee flexed (dashboard injury) or hyperextension. Pain is ill-defined with minimal swelling; posterior drawer, sag sign and reverse Lachman are positive. It usually involves other posterolateral structures; PT and bracing, with surgery for rotary instability or PLC injuries.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 27 year old male football athlete pivots with his left knee as he changes direction to the right. He feels his knee "move" as it gives way. The athlete collapses to the ground and is unable to weight bear due to significant pain and swelling.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is B. The lecture follows the case with its "ACL Injury" section. The mechanism is the one the lecture gives for a non-contact ACL tear (60-80%): cutting or pivoting while decelerating. The knee "gives way" (the lecture's "instability" or "giving out"), and the swelling is significant at once - the lecture's immediate swelling / hemarthrosis, and in the traumatic knee pain section (Part Two) an ACL tear sits among the injuries that swell within 6 hours. An MCL sprain (A) comes from a valgus collision and swells minimally or not at all. A PCL tear (C) needs a blow to the front of the tibia with the knee flexed, or hyperextension, and gives minimal swelling. A meniscal tear (D) comes from twisting on a planted foot but swells late or on and off, not immediately.

preamble.html: A 23 year old male ice hockey athlete falls awkwardly to the ice while his skate is caught up with another player. His knee rotates and he suffers immediate medial pain. There is no obvious initial swelling but develops a moderate amount of swelling later on that night.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is D. The lecture follows the case with "Meniscal Injuries". The mechanism is the lecture's for a meniscal tear: rotation or twisting with the foot planted (here the skate is caught). The pain is at the medial joint line, and the swelling is delayed - the lecture's "delayed or intermittent swelling/effusions", and in the traumatic knee pain section (Part Two) meniscal injuries swell after 6 hours. The medial meniscus is the one that tears more often, because it is fixed to the tibial collateral ligament. An ACL tear (A) swells immediately (hemarthrosis). An MCL sprain (B) also gives medial pain, but it is caused by a valgus collision and swells minimally or not at all. A PCL tear (C) needs a blow to the front of the flexed tibia, or hyperextension.
