stem: A patient presents with a large swelling at the elbow. On the lateral elbow radiograph the osseous structures are normal, and there is a well-defined, low-density oval mass within the soft tissues, causing anterior displacement of the overlying soft tissues. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? (stem assembled from the lecture, leaving out the caption and annotation that name the diagnosis; the lecture poses no question)
answer:
The correct answer is D. The module's own reveal (page 46): based on its low density and well-defined appearance, the mass was suspected to be a large lipoma, later confirmed with CT or MRI. Its lesson is that normal-looking bones do not exclude pathology, so the soft tissues must always be checked.

  • Joint effusion shows as the posterior fat pad sign (a visible posterior fat pad, always abnormal) inside the joint, not as a soft-tissue mass displacing tissue anteriorly.
  • Olecranon bursa swelling sits over the posterior olecranon (the bursa swells with inflammation or bleeding), not in the anterior soft tissues.
  • Giant cell tumour of bone is a lesion of the bone itself: an expanded bone with a large lytic lesion and thinned cortex (the module's example is in the distal radius). Here the bones are normal.

preamble.html: A 18 year old female presents with a three month history of worsening bilateral anterior knee pain. There was no injury but she recently started running. stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

A popliteal cyst (D) is a swelling behind the knee.

One of the athletes attempts a jump shot, but as she comes down an opponent lands on the outside of her knee, forcing the lower leg away from her body. She develops immediate onset medial knee pain with minimal swelling. What is the most likely injured ligament?
answer: The correct answer is B. MCL – the valgus force stretches the medial collateral ligament causing a strain. ACL can be affected in the unhappy triad (ACL, medial meniscus and MCL) however those typically produce significant swelling and higher intensity mechanism of injury. PCL is more often injured in hyperextension or dashboard injuries. LCL is more commonly injured in varus force injuries.

stem: You are working in your local Emergency Department. The next patient is 23-year-old male soccer player with a LEFT KNEE injury. While pivoting to avoid a defender, he felt a ‘pop’ as his knee gave way. His coach helped him off the field and he did not return to play. He reported swelling but is unsure when it started, and he has been unable to weight bear on his left leg. He is otherwise healthy with no medications or allergies. Please select all potential diagnoses this patient could have:
answer: The correct answers are A, B, E, J, L, and M. Acute meniscal tear Acute meniscal tears typically occur during twisting injuries (i.e. a flexed knee is rotated with the corresponding foot planted). Chronic degenerative tears occur in older patients with minimal twisting or stress. Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury The ACL is the most commonly injured ligament of the knee. Approximately 70% of injuries occur with a noncontact mechanism (e.g. sudden deceleration, change in direction, or pivoting/landing with rotation and valgus collapse of the knee). Contact-related ACL injuries usually occur from a direct blow causing hyperextension or valgus deformation of the knee. Crystal arthropathy Crystal arthropathy is the accumulation of tiny crystals in one or more joints. The knee is most commonly involved in pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition). Gout (monosodium urate crystal deposition) can also occur in the knee. Attacks are characterized by severe pain, redness, swelling and disability. Inflammatory arthropathy Inflammatory arthropathy refers to an influx of inflammatory cells into the synovial membrane or fluid. This causes pain, swelling, reduced mobility and functional impairment in one or more joints. This is usually associated with another systemic condition (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis, spondyloarthropathy, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, preceding extraarticular infection, etc.) Knee (tibiofemoral) dislocation with multi-ligament injury Knee dislocations are infrequent but potentially limb-threatening. They are caused by high energy trauma (e.g. motor vehicle collision) and are associated with multiple knee ligament injuries. This is a surgical emergency that requires immediate reduction followed by careful neurovascular assessment. These can be missed if the knee spontaneously reduces, as x-rays may appear normal. Lateral collateral ligament (LCL) sprain Isolated injuries of the LCL are among the least common of knee injuries. They occur when the joint is struck from the inside (varus stress). More commonly, LCL injuries occur in combination with posterolateral corner and multi-ligament injuries. Medial collateral ligament (MCL) sprain The MCL is commonly injured in contact and collision sports, or those that require twisting and torque of the lower extremity. They occur via direct valgus stress from a blow to the lateral aspect, or via indirect stress through abduction or rotation of the lower leg (e.g. shoe catches on playing surface). Femoral shaft fracture Fractures of the femoral shaft in young adults result from high energy forces (e.g. motor vehicle collision). They can cause extensive hemorrhage and shock may develop. There is a well-documented correlation between femur fractures and soft tissue injuries of the ipsilateral knee (partial of complete anterior or posterior cruciate ligament tears or meniscal injuries in 20-50% of cases). Osteoarthritis Osteoarthritis is common in the middle-aged or older person. It is typically characterized by joint pain, stiffness and reduced mobility. It starts with a predictable, sharp pain that eventually limits high-impact activities. As the disease progresses, pain becomes more constant with episodic stiffness or swelling that affects daily activities. Patellar dislocation Lateral patellar dislocations are most common, although medial or superior are described. They occur when the foot is planted, and a rotatory force is applied to the flexed knee in valgus (e.g. twirling in dance or swing a baseball bat). Direct trauma to the medial knee may also result in lateral patellar dislocation. Patellar tendon rupture Patellar tendon ruptures occur after sudden, strong contraction of the quadriceps muscles (e.g. landing from a high jump, changing direction at high speed). Conditions that weaken collagen put the tendon at risk, such as systemic illness (e.g. lupus, rheumatoid, diabetes), local degenerative change (e.g. tendinopathy or prior injury), or iatrogenic (e.g. corticosteroid injection, fluroquinolones, etc.). Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) tear Most PCL injuries occur in association with multi-ligament injuries after high energy trauma. The typical mechanism is a posteriorly directed force applied to a flexed knee (e.g. the classic ‘dashboard injury’). In athletes, PCL injuries can occur from a fall onto a flexed knee while the foot is plantarflexed or a direct blow to the anterior knee. Tibial plateau fracture Closed tibial fractures are common long-bone fractures. They can occur from significant direct trauma (e.g. motor vehicle collisions), knee hyperextension (e.g. collision during contact sport causing hyperextension) and twisting motions in the elderly or osteoporotic individuals. Tibial fracture is the most common injury associated with acute compartment syndrome of an extremity.

stem: What is the most commonly injured ligament of the ankle?
answer: The correct answer is D. The anterior talofibular ligament — injured during hyper-inversion of the ankle, which is the common mechanism. See ankle sprain.

lecture: Ankle & foot injuries and the imaging rules
lectureMeta: Workbook Q39, Q46-Q48. Tests [[01.2 - Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot]], [[02 - Lower Extremity Radiology]].
stem: Which of these patients requires further assessment and an x-ray?

options.html: An 18-year-old female trips over a soccer ball while playing pick-up in a park. She is unable to weight bear on her left leg following the injury and is partially carried and driven to UH to see you. In the emergency department she still cannot weight bear to let you see her gait.
A 26-year-old male comes in limping from a construction site. He can slightly weight bear during his limping. On examination you note tenderness in the last 4 cm of lateral malleolus.
A 45-year-female comes in after tripping while getting out of the shower. On examination she has marked tenderness over the base of the 5th metatarsal.
All of the patients above need an ankle or foot X-ray series

answer:
The correct answer is D. Apply the Ottawa Foot and Ankle Rules:

  • Ankle series if unable to weight bear immediately post-trauma AND in the emergency room → patient A
  • Ankle series if pain over the bottom 6 cm of the medial OR lateral malleolus → patient B (4 cm falls inside 6 cm)
  • Foot series if pain over the base of the 5th metatarsal or the navicular bone → patient C

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Arthritis & Pain
lecture: Ankle & foot injuries and the imaging rules
lectureMeta: Workbook Q39, Q46-Q48. Tests [[01.2 - Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot]], [[02 - Lower Extremity Radiology]].
stem: A patient comes to you after rolling her ankle. You note that she is not able to weight bear and so you send her for an x-ray. Which of the following are incorrect management?

options.html: You should image the ankle properly with an AP, lateral and mortise view
You find that the patient has an ankle with an approximate displacement of her medial malleolus by 1 mm, with the mortise undisplaced. You decide to manage her with conservative treatment

You find that the patient has an ankle with bi-malleolar fracture, but the mortise is not displaced, and the medial malleolus displaced under 2 mm. This patient should be considered for surgical management.
Ankle fractures classified as B and C are regarded as 'unstable'
All of the above are true

answer:
The correct answer is E — all of the above are true.

  • A — AP, lateral and mortise are the normal ankle series.
  • B — the findings meet the criteria for non-operative treatment: (i) single malleolus involvement, (ii) mortise undisplaced, (iii) <2 mm of malleolar displacement.
  • C — correctly escalates, because it involves a bimalleolar fracture (failing criterion i).
  • D — Weber categories: A = fracture below the syndesmosis, B = fracture at the syndesmosis, C = fracture above the malleolus. With fractures below the syndesmosis and only 1 malleolus involved, the ankle is relatively stable and can likely be managed conservatively — so B and C are the unstable ones.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Arthritis & Pain
lecture: Ankle & foot injuries and the imaging rules
lectureMeta: Workbook Q39, Q46-Q48. Tests [[01.2 - Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot]], [[02 - Lower Extremity Radiology]].
stem: A patient comes to you following a long run in the woods. They complain of having stepped into a pot hole and having their right foot forcefully pushed up toward their shin (dorsiflexed) and hearing a 'pop'. Following she had a great deal of pain. On examination you note a swollen painful ankle with a concentration of swelling on the back of the ankle and heel. On examination you find she has 5- strength in dorsiflexion, eversion and inversion, and a 1 in plantar flexion. What statement is correct?

options.html: The patient appears to have sustained a L4-5 injury, and is likely to display what is called a 'drop foot'.
The patient likely has a likely ankle sprain. The side whether talofibular ligaments or deltoid ligaments have not yet been determined by this examination.
Patient seems to be suffering from a common runner's injury called 'plantar fasciitis'
This patient would be expected to have a positive Thompson test, and may have a history of gout and seronegative arthropathies.

answer:
The correct answer is D. This is an Achilles tendon rupture — suspected from the isolated loss of plantar flexor strength (grade 1), the characteristic swelling at the back of the heel, and the history of forceful dorsiflexion. A positive Thompson test confirms it. There is also an association with chronic tendonitis seen in patients with gout and seronegative arthropathies, though that history is not required.

  • B is possible with this mechanism, but the specific loss of plantar flexor tone, the location of swelling, and no pain over the medial or lateral ankle argue against a simple ankle sprain.
  • C — plantar fasciitis was possibly present in a runner, but would not produce this swelling or loss of plantar flexor strength.

See Achilles tendinopathy.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Arthritis & Pain
lectureMeta: Workbook Q11, Q16-Q17, Q24, Q66. Tests [[03 - Nerve Injury]].
stem: Neuropathic pain is:

options.html: Pain caused by abnormal neural activity occurring in the absence of disease
Pain caused from stretching of visceral tissues resulting in poorly localized cramping pain
Pain resulting from local tissue damage that is well localized but with variable descriptions

answer:
The correct answer is A. Neuropathic pain is pain caused by abnormal neural activity occurring in the absence of disease.

The distractors are the two nociceptive subtypes:

  • B → visceral nociceptive pain (stretching of visceral tissue; poorly localized, cramping)
  • C → somatic nociceptive pain (local tissue damage; well localized, variable descriptors)

See 05 - Neuropathic Pain and Q65 for the symptom list.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Arthritis & Pain
lectureMeta: Workbook Q11, Q16-Q17, Q24, Q66. Tests [[03 - Nerve Injury]].
stem: Wallerian degeneration is the process of _____ nerve tract degeneration _____ to the site of injury.
answer: The correct answer is D. Wallerian degeneration is the breakdown of nerve tissue that occurs when a nerve is transected through traumatic injury. Degeneration starts at the site of injury and progresses distally (anterograde), obliterating the nerve segment distal to the injury. See Q66 for where this fits among neuropraxia/axonotmesis/neurotmesis.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Arthritis & Pain
lectureMeta: Workbook Q11, Q16-Q17, Q24, Q66. Tests [[03 - Nerve Injury]].
stem: Nerves repair at a rate of:
answer: The correct answer is A. 1 mm/day ≈ 1 inch/month. Both halves of that equivalence are worth carrying, since exam options are written in either unit.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Arthritis & Pain
lectureMeta: Workbook Q11, Q16-Q17, Q24, Q66. Tests [[03 - Nerve Injury]].
stem: Localize the following physical exam findings: The patient is stepping with their affected foot in a plantar flexed position during swing phase of normal gait and makes contact with their forefoot. The patient has MRC grade 3 strength in dorsiflexion and 4+ in plantar flexion.

options.html: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh

answer: The correct answer is B. The patient has a foot drop on gait analysis with profound weakness of the dorsiflexors (grade 3) and relatively preserved plantar flexion (4+). This lesion localizes to the common fibular/peroneal nerve — or the deep fibular/peroneal nerve for the anterior compartment specifically. See common peroneal neuropathy.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Arthritis & Pain
lectureMeta: Workbook Q11, Q16-Q17, Q24, Q66. Tests [[03 - Nerve Injury]].
stem: Which of the following correctly describes neuropraxia?

options.html: Damage to a neuron's outer sheath progressing to Wallerian degeneration, often resulting from severe crush injuries
Complete severance of both the nerve and its sheath
Temporary loss of sensory and motor function from transient neural ischemia & edema. Patients usually make a full recovery

answer:
The correct answer is C. The three-tier classification, with all three options accounted for:

GradeDefinitionOption
NeuropraxiaTemporary loss of sensory and motor function from transient neural ischemia & edema; usually full recoveryC
AxonotmesisDamage to the outer sheath, progressing to Wallerian degeneration; severe crush injuriesA
NeurotmesisComplete severance of both nerve and sheathB

See Q16 for Wallerian degeneration and Q17 for the recovery rate.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q33, Q37, Q49, Q56. Tests [[04 - Acute Monoarthritis]], [[06 - Osteoarthritis]], [[07 - Approach to Polyarthritis]], [[08 - Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis]].
stem: A 73-year-old patient comes to you with a several year history of bilateral knee pain that is worse on the right side. On examination you find MRC 5 for knee extension and flexion as well as a normal neurologic examination. On palpation you see his knees are slightly swollen but not red or hot. You find there is joint line tenderness and crepitus with passive movement. There is no sign of patellar apprehension or grinding. Anterior and posterior drawer tests are negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: Central medial meniscal tear from twisting

answer:
The correct answer is D. Arthritis — the patient's age 73 (over 50), the long history without trauma, crepitus on movement and joint line tenderness all point there.

B is the most likely meniscal injury for an elderly patient, but there is no history of trauma and no evidence of true locking. C is unlikely with no grinding or patellar apprehension on exam.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Arthritis & Pain
lectureMeta: Workbook Q33, Q37, Q49, Q56. Tests [[04 - Acute Monoarthritis]], [[06 - Osteoarthritis]], [[07 - Approach to Polyarthritis]], [[08 - Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis]].
stem: A patient comes to you with an antalgic gait and some swelling over the great toe of the left foot. She had become upset during a personal matter and kicked her door. Upon examination you find that the toe is extremely painful for the patient and you decide to get an x-ray. You see a transverse fracture of the distal phalange of the great toe with no involvement of articular surface. How do you manage?

options.html: Do nothing, toe injuries generally require no treatment
Buddy tape the great toe to the next toe
Activity modification, physio and no weight bearing

answer:
The correct answer is B. Buddy taping is appropriate when there is no displacement and no involvement of the articular surface. Note the two escalation triggers embedded in that rule:

  • displacement → surgery
  • articular surface involvement → foot and toe cast

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Arthritis & Pain
lectureMeta: Workbook Q33, Q37, Q49, Q56. Tests [[04 - Acute Monoarthritis]], [[06 - Osteoarthritis]], [[07 - Approach to Polyarthritis]], [[08 - Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis]].
stem: A 16 y.o. F. pianist came in with progressive swollen joints (multiple) over the last three months, more than 6 joints involved in her hands, they feel warm and tender on palpation, what are your top 3 differential diagnoses?
answer:
The correct answers are B, E, F. The patient demographic (female, late teen) fits RA, SLE and JIA best. The condition is chronic (over three months) with multiple joints involved.

Each exclusion turns on one feature:

  • A Infectious — ruled out by the chronic, polyarticular course
  • C AS — more likely in the lower back
  • D Acute gout — usually one joint, and this is a chronic patient
  • G Chondrosarcoma — a large mass around bigger joints, not a polyarthritis

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Arthritis & Pain
lectureMeta: Workbook Q33, Q37, Q49, Q56. Tests [[04 - Acute Monoarthritis]], [[06 - Osteoarthritis]], [[07 - Approach to Polyarthritis]], [[08 - Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis]].
stem: A 50-year-old female patient comes to you complaining of aching in her knees and feet that has been occurring daily, she has minor pains in the morning but the pain progresses with activity throughout the day especially with walking. In history you get the impression that this pain is bothersome but is not limiting her function. On exam you notice slight bowing (varus deformity) in her knees. Overall outside the pain, the patient does not complain of fever, nausea, or fatigue. You order a radiograph to assess her knees and ankles, what do you expect?

options.html: Subchondral sclerosis, cysts, osteophytes, eccentric cartilage loss, loose bodies
Osteopenia, bony erosions, soft tissue swelling

answer:
The correct answer is A. We suspect osteoarthritis because of the daily pain that progresses through the day and worsens with activity, supported by the absence of systemic symptoms (fever, fatigue, nausea) that would point toward rheumatoid arthritis.

Note that B and C are the RA radiographic picture — osteopenia, bony erosions, soft tissue swelling and symmetric joint space narrowing — whereas OA gives eccentric cartilage loss with osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Arthritis & Pain
lectureMeta: Workbook Q41, Q43-Q45. Tests [[11 - Body Pain]].
stem: Which of the following statements is true?

options.html: Repetitive strain injuries (RSI) are caused by maximal or over the maximal exertion
Around 5% of the Canadian General population experience chronic pain
Opioid analgesics can result in Respiratory depression, mental clouding, nausea/vomiting, constipation, drug tolerance
The majority of the chronic pain are caused through the nociceptive pathway whereas the acute pain are usually neuropathic

answer:
The correct answer is C. All of those are side effects of opioids. Each other option has a specific error:

  • A — RSI is caused by submaximal exertion over a period of time without recovery (sitting in a funny position for too long), not maximal exertion.
  • B — around 30%, not 5%, of the Canadian general population experience chronic pain.
  • D — backwards: chronic pain is more neuropathic, acute pain more nociceptive.

See 01 - Understanding and Managing Chronic Pain.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Arthritis & Pain
lectureMeta: Workbook Q41, Q43-Q45. Tests [[11 - Body Pain]].
stem: What is the dose referred to as the 'watchful dose' in opioid management?
answer:
The correct answer is D. 90 mg/day of morphine or equivalent is the "watchful dose" — where significant increases in side effects such as constipation appear, and where the risk of drug diversion/sale rises.

To manage risk at this level, some suggest titrating opioids for a 30% increase in function or reduction in pain.

C is the old answer: in previous years 200 mg was the watchful dose; the updated guidelines moved it to 90 mg.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Arthritis & Pain
lectureMeta: Workbook Q41, Q43-Q45. Tests [[11 - Body Pain]].
stem: Which of the following is false about ASA?

options.html: Indication: pain, fever, anti-inflammatory in high doses, anti-thrombotic in low dose
Contraindications include hypersensitivity reactions to NSAIDs and children with fever (risks of Reyes syndrome)
Adverse drug reaction includes GI bleeding, tinnitus in high doses, hypersensitivities, prolonged bleeding
Aspirin has little to no toxicity and mortality risk

answer:
The correct answer is D. There is significant risk of overdose with aspirin, due to rapid saturation of the drug's conjugation system — once conjugation saturates, kinetics shift and levels climb disproportionately.

A-C are all accurate: dose-dependent indications, contraindication in children with fever because of Reye syndrome, and the ADR profile including tinnitus at high doses.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Arthritis & Pain
lectureMeta: Workbook Q41, Q43-Q45. Tests [[11 - Body Pain]].
stem: Which of the following does not have anti-inflammatory effects?
answer: The correct answer is B. Acetaminophen has antipyretic and analgesic effects but essentially no anti-inflammatory effects — which is exactly what separates it from the NSAIDs. All the other listed drugs do have anti-inflammatory effects.

answer: The correct answer is A, B, D. consider surgery since she has multiple risk factors for progression (girl, premenarchal, thoracic spine). Pain is rarely a presenting feature for scoliosis.

stem: Patient with a family history of neurofibromatosis presents with a mass that is less than 5cm, tethered, and deep on the hip. What is the best sampling method for this lesion?
answer: The correct answer is B. suspect sarcoma, so best sampling method is core biopsy. FNAB cannot provide cell organization and structure. Incisional is more invasive than core biopsy. Excisional biopsy is not ideal for sarcoma.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. Patient with a family history of neurofibromatosis presents with a mass that is less than 5cm, tethered, and deep on the hip.

stem: The biopsy sample confirms sarcoma. What are the next management steps?
answer: The correct answer is B, C, E. treatment is pre op radiation, then surgery. These tumors are resistant to chemotherapy, so no chemo done. Post op chest CT important to monitor recovery.

stem: Why is it important to have multiple Xray views when assessing a fracture? (select all that apply)

options.html: To pick up microfractures that may only be seen in one view
To differentiate between a transverse and linear fracture
To assess whether an oblique fracture is actually a spiral fracture
To check whether tendons are involved in an avulsion fracture

answer: The correct answer is A, C, E. some microfractures may only be seen in one view. A transverse and linear fracture are very different, and can be differentiated from a single view. A spiral fracture may look like an oblique fracture in one view, so it is important to obtain another view to differentiate the two. Tendons cannot be seen well on Xrays. Rotational fractures usually need two views to look at joints proximally and distally to interpret the degree and type of rotation.

stem: Which of the following is true for fracture healing?

options.html: Primary healing is healing that comes spontaneously and seen more commonly
Bony callus forms at fracture site, then revascularization occurs
Distal humerus takes longer to heal than proximal humerus
Malunion refers to no healing in 6-9 months
Healing takes longer if the fracture is extraarticular since there is no synovial fluid involved

answer: The correct answer is C. A is wrong because this describes secondary healing, primary healing is the contact healing after closed reduction or ORIF. B is wrong because revascularization occurs first, then formation of bony callus occurs after. C is correct. D describes nonunion. E is wrong because intraarticular fractures take a longer time to heal.

stem: 50 year old patient presents to the emergency department following a motor vehicle accident. Xrays show that there is a talar neck fracture. The patient undergoes ORIF. What complication will the patient most likely experience following this injury?
answer: The correct answer is A. posttraumatic arthritis is the most likely complication following ankle fracture. Osteonecrosis is possible, but not as likely as posttraumatic arthritis. Osteoarthritis and heterotopic ossification are not likely in the ankle.

stem: Patient presents with an open tibial fracture with a skin defect measuring 5cm. Which of the following are true? (select all that apply)

options.html: There is an increased chance of nonunion and infection
Obtain tetanus status and administer tetanus prophylaxis
Take a swab and wait for culture results before administering antibiotics
Contact plastic surgery to perform flap surgery

answer: The correct answer is A, B. there is an increased chance of complications (infection, nonunion, time to union) for open fractures. It is important to get tetanus status and prophylaxis for all open fractures. Do not wait for culture to administer antibiotics. Since this is a grade 2 open fracture, there is no need for flap surgery.

stem: You are in the emergency room assessing Rachel Green, a 31 year old female. Rachel was driving her friend’s Porsche at high speed on the 401 when the car in front of her braked suddenly. Rachel collided into the car in front of her. On your exam, you notice Rachel has some mild knee pain, minimal swelling of her right knee and decreased range of motion. Given the mechanism of injury, what knee ligament did Rachel most likely injure?
answer: The correct answer is D. This is a classic dashboard injury causing the tibia to move posteriorly relative to the femur when the knee is flexed. Patients typically present with poorly defined pain and minimal swelling.

stem: Tobiloba is a 19 year old woman coming to see you in the family medicine clinic with gradually worsening bilateral anterior knee pain. She describes the pain as deep and aching. She first noticed the pain when she increased her hurdles training volume, and initially the pain was brought on by exercise. However, the pain is now brought on when she climbs stairs and stands up after prolonged periods of sitting. Based on the most likely diagnosis, what would you offer Tobiloba? Choose all that are correct.
answer: The correct answer is A, C, D, E. Given the presentation and the demographics of this case, Tobiloba most likely has patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS). Because PFPS is related to increased Q angle, physiotherapy may focus on quadriceps strengthening (especially vastus medialis) to prevent lateral translation of the patella during knee flexion. Knee surgery is not indicated. Activity modifications are indicated, and bracing and taping may also help prevent lateral patellar translation.

stem: You are a family medicine resident seeing Kavi, 58 years old, who complains to you about pain in their legs. They have aching pain in both legs that sometimes feels itchy. Kavi works in customer service and finds the pain to be worse after a long shift standing. On physical exam, you see dilated, tortuous veins on both legs. Which of the following is not recommended for Kavi?
answer: The correct answer is A, B, D, E. Kavi has varicose veins. Exercise, compression stockings, and daily elevation of the legs can help return the blood towards the heart. Laser therapy damages the varicose veins, causing formation of scar tissue and eventual disappearance of the vein. Daily hot water soaks are NOT recommended as they can further vasodilation and venous stasis.

stem: Milica is a 30 year old woman in your family medicine clinic seeking help for pain on the dorsum of her right foot which radiates to the space between her first and second toes. She recently took on a job at a ski resort where she teaches ski lessons for six hours a day. Which nerve has Milica most likely compressed?
answer: The correct answer is D. Tight boots such as ski boots can compress the deep fibular nerve where it passes under the extensor retinaculum.

stem: How does physical activity affect the cardiovascular system? Check all that are correct.
answer:
The correct answer is A, D.

From 08 - Physical Activity Prescription. The lecture lists the cardiovascular benefits of regular activity: ↑ oxygen uptake, ↑ oxygen utilization, ↑ endothelial function, ↑ plasma volume and ↓ blood viscosity, with ↑ stroke volume, ↓ resting heart rate and ↓ blood pressure on the heart side.

  • A, D are on that list verbatim.
  • B fails on the word during: the ↓ BP is a chronic training effect. Acutely, blood pressure rises with exertion, which is why the notes require BP under 180/100 before starting and warn that strenuous resistance work can push LV pressure over 300 mmHg.
  • C is the reverse of the lecture: viscosity falls.

stem: Akbar is a 56 year old patient interested in adding physical activity to his lifestyle. He comes to you for advice because he is fairly sedentary and has a history of hypertension, with average readings of 185/100. Which of the following would you NOT recommend?

options.html: At least one rest day per week

answer: The correct answer is A. ACE inhibitor or calcium channel blocker will help control Akbar’s hypertension to make exercise safe. Including a warmup of 15minutes and a cool-down of 10minutes is an important consideration for patients with hypertension. One rest day per week will help Akbar avoid injury. Isometric exercises, overhead exercises and supine exercises are not recommended for patients with hypertension.

stem: Blanche, a 55 year old woman, comes to your walk-in clinic seeking help for pain on the bottom of her foot. The pain localizes to her heel and she tells you the pain is the worst when she gets out of bed in the morning and when she goes for a run. Based on your suspected diagnosis, which of the following would you not recommend for Blanche?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Blanche most likely has plantar fasciitis. While A, B, C, and E are important non-pharmacological interventions, corticosteroid injections do not play a role.

stem: Pes planus commonly occurs after an injury to which of the following muscles?
answer: The correct answer is A. While peroneus longus and tibialis anterior also play a role in supporting the medial longitudinal arch, the main contributor is tibialis posterior, and thus injury to tibialis posterior is a common cause of pes planus.

stem: A 50-year-old woman has heel pain that is worst with her first steps in the morning and after sitting. She is tender at the medial calcaneal tuberosity and passive dorsiflexion of the toes reproduces the pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is C. Plantar fasciitis is a clinical diagnosis: plantar heel pain worse when initiating walking (first steps in the morning) plus point tenderness at the origin of the plantar fascia on the medial calcaneal tuberosity, often with a tight Achilles. Achilles tendinopathy hurts at the posterior heel near its insertion.

stem: A 23-year-old basketball player lands on another player's foot, rolling the ankle into inversion with the foot plantarflexed. Which ligament is most likely injured?
answer: The correct answer is D. Most ankle sprains are lateral: inversion with plantarflexion (the least stable position) injures the ATFL most often, then the CFL, then the PTFL. The anterior drawer test assesses the ATFL. Medial sprains involve the deltoid ligament.

stem: A 68-year-old man with diabetes has had a foot ulcer for several months. It is now infected, with erythema and purulence but no systemic features. Because the ulcer is chronic, the infection is likely polymicrobial. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
answer: The correct answer is E. A wound alone does not mean infection. Mild, monomicrobial infections (S. aureus, S. pyogenes) can be treated with cefazolin; chronic ulcers are more likely polymicrobial (including gram-negatives) and need amoxicillin-clavulanate. Pip-tazo is for Pseudomonas. Start imaging with x-ray, then MRI for osteomyelitis; debridement is often needed.

stem: A 70-year-old man has a hot, red, swollen knee and a fever. Aspiration shows cloudy fluid with gram-positive cocci in clusters. He has no MRSA risk factors. Along with blood cultures, what is the most appropriate management?

options.html: Oral cephalexin and repeat aspiration in a week
IV cefazolin plus irrigation and debridement
IV antibiotics alone without joint drainage

answer: The correct answer is B. Septic arthritis is an emergency: aspirate for the 3 Cs (cell count, culture/gram stain, crystals) and call ortho. Usual source is hematogenous seeding with S. aureus or streptococci. Treat with cefazolin (Ancef) 2 g IV q8h plus irrigation and debridement; vancomycin + ceftriaxone if MRSA risk.

stem: A 34-year-old daycare worker develops symmetric pain and swelling of the small joints of both hands a week after a febrile illness. Her CBC shows a new anemia. Which infection is most likely?
answer: The correct answer is A. Viral arthritis tends to be polyarticular, while bacterial arthritis is usually monoarticular. For an infectious polyarthritis think of endocarditis and viruses: parvovirus B19 (associated with anemia), hepatitis B/C and HIV. Gonococcal, Lyme and TB arthritis classically cause a large-joint monoarthritis.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: "My Knee Hurts": 28 yo M with acute onset R knee pain. The knee is swollen and red. Joint fluid: synovial, Left Knee, Bloody, nucleated cells 21.500, neutrophils 90.0%, monocytoid 10.0%. He also has the skin lesions shown: a small pustule on the palm and a necrotic pustule on a toe.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: Lyme arthritis after a tick bite
Acute gouty arthritis of the knee

answer: The correct answer is B. The notes do not name the diagnosis in the case itself; the answer table that follows does, where disseminated gonococcal infection is tenosynovitis, dermatitis with a pustular rash, and polyarthralgia in the young with multiple partners (gonococcal arthritis: large-joint monoarthritis, knee, wrist, ankle). Workup: blood culture, gonorrhea NAAT or culture of urine, rectum and throat, joint fluid (positive in 50%); treatment ceftriaxone for 10-14 days. Lyme arthritis (A) is a large-joint monoarthritis without a pustular rash. Reactive arthritis (C) follows a gut or genitourinary infection by days to weeks, with conjunctivitis and urethritis. Gout (D) gives urate crystals, which the notes say distinguish it from septic arthritis.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: OM Case #1: 55 yo M with 5 day history of severe 9/10 lower back pain. Afebrile, HR 92, BP 140/70. Physical exam: 5/5 Strength in lower limbs, N reflexes, N sensation; N Anal tone, No saddle anesthesia.

stem: Which of the following are the most appropriate next steps? (the notes reveal "Next Steps" without posing a question; stem written for this bank)

options.html: Plain X-ray of the lumbar spine and reassurance
CT of the lumbar spine and oral analgesia
Nuclear medicine tagged white cell scan alone
Blood cultures and an MRI of the spine

answer: The correct answer is D. The notes: "Next Steps: Blood Cultures, MRI Spine" (and a word on spinal biopsy). His MRI showed bone marrow edema and enhancement in L3 and L4 with irregular endplates, spondylodiscitis and osteomyelitis, raising paravertebral and epidural abscess; treatment is 6 weeks of antibiotics, IV vancomycin and ceftriaxone, with neurosurgery if there is neurologic compromise. X-ray and CT (A, B) are "not sensitive enough"; MRI is the most sensitive and the one for vertebral osteomyelitis; a tagged white cell scan (C) takes 2 days.

options.html: Offloading the pressure and debriding it
A superficial swab to choose an antibiotic
A long course of oral antibiotics alone
A repeat MRI every two weeks to monitor

answer: The correct answer is A. The lecture assesses this ulcer by chronicity, offloading and debridement, and its treatment section asks about vascular supply (revascularization?), chronicity (debridement?), and patient engagement and offloading: "ANTIBIOTICS ALONE WILL NOT SAVE YOU" (C). Just because there is a wound does not mean it is infected, and if you swab any wound you WILL find bacteria (B). MRI stays abnormal despite resolution, and imaging is not routinely repeated in a patient who is improving (D).

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Diabetic Foot Infection: Case 2. A patient with diabetes has the foot shown: a large necrotic wound over the dorsum of the foot with surrounding erythema, and the features of a severe infection.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management? (stem written for this bank; the lecture gives the plan for "Severe Infections" without posing a question)

options.html: Superficial swab, then oral cephalexin and review in one week
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate alone, with no surgical review
Wait for an MRI before starting any antibiotic or consulting

answer: The correct answer is C. The lecture, severe infections: exclude necrotizing fasciitis, blood cultures, swab only if a good (deeper) specimen can be obtained, consider calling orthopedics (or vascular), and start piperacillin-tazobactam (± vancomycin if MRSA history or risks). Oral cefazolin-class drugs (A) are for mild, monomicrobial infection, and a superficial swab always grows bacteria. Amoxicillin-clavulanate (B) covers a chronic polymicrobial ulcer but not a severe infection, and antibiotics alone will not save you. Imaging starts with an X-ray, and a severe infection is not left untreated for it (D).

stem: A 65 yo M with type 2 diabetes, hypertension and obesity, presents to the clinic with a hot, red swollen right knee. He has no documented fever, but is unable to weight bear. This morning he reported chills. What empiric parenteral antibiotic therapy would you choose for this patient?
answer: The correct answer is D. You're worried about a septic arthritis in this patient. Cefazolin provides appropriate coverage of the most likely infectious agents (S. aureus and streptococcus), and can be changed if needed once culture results are available.

stem: A 45 yo M presents to hospital with new onset lumbar back pain. He reports the pain is 10/10. Yesterday morning he had fever and chills. He does not report any lower limb weakness, or bladder or bowel dysfunction. He has a history of opioid use, and reports injecting drugs.
answer: The correct answers are A, B, and C. CBC, CRP and blood cultures will help to determine the presence of an infection and the causative agent, and CBC and CRP may need to be monitored over time to assess his progress with treatment. CK and urine culture will not be helpful in making the diagnosis of infection (particularly in the absence of any urinary symptoms). Urine tox screen may be needed for other reasons, but will not help elucidate the cause of his current symptoms.

stem: Moishe is a 62 yo M with type 2 diabetes. His most recent A1C was 9.2%. He is prescribed Metformin 1 g PO BID, but often forgets to take it. He recently started a new job as a grocery store cashier, and now spends 8 hours per shift on his feet. He wears running shoes to work that he ties tightly so they don't rub his feet. He purchased some new foot orthotics as recommended by his podiatrist. Each night he inspects his feet. Which of the following are significant steps that Moishe has taken to prevent the development of diabetic foot ulcer? (choose all that apply)
answer: The correct answers are A, C, and D. Visiting a professional who can care for the feet is very helpful in preventing diabetic foot ulcers. This ensures regular foot checks (in addition to those that Moishe is doing on his own) and quick response to any developing issues. Orthoses can help protect any vulnerable areas of the feet from breakdown. Just having a metformin prescription doesn't help overly - regular compliance with the recommended dose will!

stem: A 25-year-old man wakes with a wrist drop after falling asleep with his arm hooked over a chair. The nerve was compressed but not cut. Which type of injury is this and what is the expected course?
answer: The correct answer is A. Compression that damages myelin with the axon intact is neurapraxia: slowed conduction, temporary, typically resolving in 6-12 weeks (radial nerve "Saturday night" palsy). Axonotmesis (crush/stretch) loses the axon, which regrows about 1 inch per month. Neurotmesis (cut) disrupts the epineurium and cannot recover without surgery.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Consider case of "numb thumb". Pt c/o frequent tingles. Exam shows diminished sensation over thumb.

stem: Two items in the DDx should include: (stem copied from the lecture, which answers it straight after; options written for this bank)

options.html: Carpal tunnel syndrome and C8 radiculopathy
Carpal tunnel syndrome and C6 radiculopathy

answer: The correct answer is C. The lecture lists them: 1. Carpal tunnel syndrome (peripheral nerve: the median nerve) and 2. C6 radiculopathy (nerve root). The lecture shows why both fit: the median nerve sensory territory and the C6 dermatome overlap over the thumb. "Your job is to figure out which Dx fits best": a mononeuropathy gives a sharp-bordered patch and weakness only in that nerve's muscles (motor to abductor pollicis brevis for the median nerve), a radiculopathy gives a fuzzy-bordered dermatome, neck pain radiating down the arm and myotome weakness (motor to biceps for C6). On the sensory maps in the lecture note, C8 (A) and the ulnar nerve (B) cover the little-finger side, not the thumb, and C7 the middle finger; the radial nerve (D) covers the back of the hand.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Onset with horseback riding trauma yesterday: ran into fence with R knee, thrown over and landed on low back; pain. Inability to dorsiflex, extend toes, evert. Plantarflexion, knee flexion weak & painful. Loss of sensation dorsum of foot. On examination: reduced pinprick sensation over the dorsum of the foot, clear borders; hip flexion, knee extension, hip adduction and abduction, plantarflexion and tibialis posterior 4+/5; dorsiflexion, extensor hallucis longus and eversion 0/5; patellar and plantar reflexes intact. Sent for EMG studies. Needle EMG is abnormal in peroneus longus, tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum brevis only; gluteus medius, the tibial-innervated muscles and the paraspinals are normal.

stem: Where does weakness come from? (the case assembled from the lecture and its EMG table, leaving out the part that names the diagnosis)

options.html: Sciatic nerve in the posterior thigh
Tibial nerve in the popliteal fossa

answer: The correct answer is B. The lecture names it: common peroneal neuropathy at the fibular head. Only the peroneal muscles (superficial: peroneus longus; deep: tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum brevis) are abnormal, the sensory loss has clear borders, and the reflexes are intact, which is a mononeuropathy: weakness of the muscles that nerve takes care of but not of other muscles from the same root that another nerve manages. An L5 radiculopathy (A) also catches gluteus medius, tibialis posterior and the paraspinals (the lecture's alternate ending). A sciatic lesion (C) would add the hamstrings, including biceps femoris short head, which is normal here. A tibial lesion (D) weakens plantarflexion and spares dorsiflexion.

preamble.html: The man with the foot drop above. Nerve conduction studies: no responses from the superficial peroneal sensory study or the peroneal motor study. stem: What Type of Nerve Injury is It? (stem copied from the lecture heading; options written for this bank)

options.html: Neurapraxia: myelin injury only, axon intact
Neurotmesis: the whole nerve has been cut
Axonotmesis: the epineurium is still intact
Axonal injury, grade not yet known

answer: The correct answer is D. The lecture: "This is an AXONAL INJURY. Can't say yet if axonotmetic or neurotmetic (would need to wait and see if it recovers spontaneously)." Dx: common peroneal axonopathy at the fibular head. Spontaneous activity at rest is denervation, which a myelin-only injury (A) does not produce (denervated muscle does not behave normally at rest). Neurotmesis (B) and axonotmesis (C) both cut the axon; what separates them is whether the epineurium is intact, and the studies cannot see that yet, only time can.

stem: Where does weakness come from? (the lecture's "Case: Alternate Ending"; stem copied from the lecture, leaving out the box that names the diagnosis)

options.html: Sciatic nerve in the posterior thigh
Superior gluteal nerve at the hip

answer: The correct answer is A. The lecture names it: L5 radiculopathy. The abnormal muscles cross several named nerves (superior gluteal, common peroneal, tibial, and the sciatic branch to semimembranosus) but share one root, and the paraspinals, supplied by the posterior primary rami, are abnormal too: a myotome, not a nerve. A common peroneal lesion (B) would leave gluteus medius, tibialis posterior and the paraspinals normal. A sciatic lesion (C) cannot explain gluteus medius or the paraspinals. A superior gluteal lesion (D) would not weaken the leg muscles.

stem: A 52-year-old man has an exquisitely painful, red first MTP joint that started overnight after a weekend of heavy drinking. Aspiration shows urate crystals. His serum uric acid today is normal. What should be done about the uric acid level?

options.html: Nothing more; a normal level excludes gout
Start allopurinol today to lower it
Repeat it once the attack has settled
Repeat it daily until it rises

answer: The correct answer is C. Serum uric acid can be normal during an acute gout attack, so check it during and again after the attack. The diagnosis rests on urate crystals in joint fluid. Triggers follow SMARTS (surgery, mechanical injury, alcohol, recent illness, travel, starting or stopping allopurinol); allopurinol prevents recurrence but is not started for the acute attack.

stem: A 78-year-old woman with knee osteoarthritis develops an acutely swollen, warm knee over a day and a low-grade fever. Aspiration shows rhomboid-shaped crystals and a negative gram stain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is D. Pseudogout (CPPD) is caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals, typically in older patients with OA, most often the knee. It is less intense than gout but lasts longer, and can cause fever, so it must be separated from sepsis by aspiration. Rhomboid crystals = CPPD; needle-shaped crystals = gout. Treat like gout (indomethacin, IA or oral steroid).

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mr. Williams' sore ankle: 62 yr old man, lives alone. Has diabetes (Metformin & Glyburide). Right knee has been replaced due to osteoarthritis. Not feeling well, left ankle has recently become much more painful, warm, and red. Recent pedicure for diabetes. Physical: temp 38.6 C, flushed and in pain. Left ankle is warm, red, and extremely painful. Cannot put much weight on the ankle.

stem: What do you want to do? (stem copied from the lecture; options written for this bank)

options.html: Check a serum uric acid and wait
Aspirate the joint and send the fluid
Inject a corticosteroid into the ankle

answer: The correct answer is C. The lecture: "Aspirate the joint (i.e. take a sample of fluid from the joint). IF THE JOINT IS RED, ASPIRATE IT!", and send it for the 3 C's: cell count, culture and sensitivity (with Gram stain), crystals. The differential for an acute hot, red monoarthritis is infection, infection, infection, gout, pseudogout, and he is febrile with diabetes and a prosthetic joint. A serum uric acid (A) cannot diagnose gout and may be normal during an attack. Allopurinol (B) is never started during an acute attack. Injecting a steroid (D) before infection is excluded treats the wrong disease: "to inject is human, to aspirate divine".

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is A. The lecture sends him to the emergency department with "Suspected left ankle infection": septic arthritis, a medical emergency. Gram-positive cocci in clusters are staphylococci, 60%+ of septic arthritis, and his risks are systemic (diabetes, age) and local (a prosthetic joint). Gout (B) needs needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals, and pseudogout (C) rhomboid positively birefringent ones; the crystals are negative. Reactive arthritis (D) is one of the rare causes and has no organisms in the joint.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mr. Williams, above: suspected left ankle infection, Gram-positive cocci in clusters, culture pending, orthopedics consulted.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management? (the notes reveal the management without posing a question; stem written for this bank)

options.html: Inject the ankle with a corticosteroid, then discharge home
Admit, urgent incision and drainage, empiric IV antibiotics
Oral colchicine, then review in the clinic in one week's time
Oral antibiotics at home until the culture result comes back

answer: The correct answer is B. The notes: admitted to hospital, taken to the OR that evening for urgent incision and drainage (I&D), "an infected joint is actually an infection in a closed space and usually requires drainage", started on empiric IV cefotaxime, with analgesia and rest. Then repeat I&D until the surgeon is confident the joint is clean, and IV antibiotics for 4-6 weeks. The MSK Infections lecture gives the usual empiric choice as cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours, or vancomycin + ceftriaxone. A steroid injection (A) and colchicine (C) treat crystal arthritis; oral antibiotics at home (D) leave a closed-space infection undrained in an emergency that can quickly cause fulminant joint damage.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mike's Toe Woes: 48 yr old married man. Works at Labatt Brewery. Hypertensive (high blood pressure) on 25 mg Hydrochlorothiazide. Two days post cholecystectomy severe pain, swelling and redness 1st MTP joint. No HCT for 2 days. Similar episode on a trip to Mexico 2 years ago. Took OTC medication which helped. The joint is aspirated. Cell Count: 15 x 109 cells per litre (inflammatory). Culture: No growth at 24 hours. Crystals: Needle shaped negatively bi-refringent crystals.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is D. The case's answer: "Diagnosis: Acute Gout", an acute inflammatory arthritis caused by uric acid crystal deposition in the joint. Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals prove it; the big toe (1st MTP) is affected in 50%; he is a man of 35-50 on a diuretic, with alcohol exposure, and the trigger is surgery (SMARTS). Pseudogout (A) has rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals and favours the knee of an older person. The culture shows no growth, against septic arthritis (B). Cellulitis (C) does not put crystals in the joint fluid.

stem: Which of the following should NOT be started during this acute attack? (the lecture teaches the acute treatment without posing a question; stem written for this bank)
answer: The correct answer is A. The lecture: allopurinol (a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, "turning off the tap") is "Do Not Start During an Acute Attack"; when it is started later, it is covered with an NSAID or colchicine and aims for the lower limit of the laboratory reference range. The acute attack is "mopped up" first with an intra-articular corticosteroid, indomethacin 50 mg PO TID (B), colchicine 0.6 mg PO q8h (C) or prednisone 30 mg OD x 2 days then reduced by 5 mg every 2 days (D).

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mary's Sore Knees: 78 year old woman lives with her husband. Has diabetes (Metformin). Has hypercholesterolemia. Has had mild chronic bilateral knee pain which has been worse with activity. After a recent brisk walk developed severe right sided knee pain and significant swelling. On examination the right knee is very swollen and noticeably warm and mildly red. She has difficulty flexing the right knee past 100 degrees. The left knee has a small effusion, it is cool and has slightly reduced flexion. Otherwise early changes of osteoarthritis (degenerative arthritis) in the hands. The knee is aspirated. Cell Count: 18 x 10^9 cells per litre (inflammatory). Culture: No growth at 24 hours. Crystals: Rhomboid shaped intracellular positively bi-refringent crystals.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is C. The notes: "Diagnosis: Acute Pseudogout", an acute inflammatory arthritis caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals. Rhomboid, intracellular, positively birefringent crystals prove it; it favours older people with osteoarthritis, and the knee is the most common joint. Gout (A) gives needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. The culture shows no growth (B). Osteoarthritis (D) is not inflammatory and gives a cool joint, while this fluid is inflammatory with crystals.

stem: A 40-year-old man has swelling of several DIP joints, one whole "sausage" toe, and pitting of his fingernails. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is B. DIP involvement points to psoriatic arthritis or OA; RA and the other CTDs usually spare the DIPs. Psoriatic arthritis adds dactylitis, enthesitis and nail changes (pitting, onycholysis) and is a clinical diagnosis. RA is symmetric small-joint arthritis of the hands and feet with more than an hour of morning stiffness.

stem: A patient presents with persistent right wrist pain and swelling. 3 weeks later, the right 2nd to 5th MCPs become affected, in addition to the existing right wrist pain. Another 6 weeks later, the left knee and left wrist also start to swell and become painful. The course of this patient’s arthritis is best described as…
answer: The correct answer is D. The patient has had symptoms for at least 9 weeks, so this is considered chronic polyarthritis. The joints symptoms are persistent and there are progressively more joints becoming involved in the disease process. This is a common pattern for rheumatoid arthritis

stem: A 24-year-old man has 6 months of low back and buttock pain that wakes him in the second half of the night, with over an hour of morning stiffness that improves with exercise. Last year he had anterior uveitis. Chest expansion is reduced. Which investigation is most useful next?
answer: The correct answer is C. Inflammatory back pain (better with movement, second-half-of-night pain, long morning stiffness) with anterior uveitis and reduced chest expansion suggests ankylosing spondylitis. Investigate with a pelvic x-ray for sacroiliitis, CRP/ESR and HLA-B27; some patients show changes only on MRI.

stem: Three weeks after an episode of urethritis, a 26-year-old man develops a painful swollen knee and ankle, red eyes and dysuria. Joint aspirate culture is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is D. Reactive arthritis follows a GI or GU infection by 1-3 weeks and is not an infection of the joint itself: "can't see" (conjunctivitis/uveitis), "can't pee" (urethritis), "can't climb a tree" (large-joint oligoarthritis). It is a clinical diagnosis and is often HLA-B27 positive.

stem: A 48-year-old woman has dry eyes, a dry mouth with dental caries, and bilateral parotid swelling. Which antibody pair is most characteristic of her likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is E. Sjögren syndrome: sicca (dry eyes and mouth), salivary gland involvement, Raynaud's, arthritis. Most patients are ANA and RF positive, and anti-Ro and anti-La are characteristic. Treatment includes artificial tears and saliva.

stem: A 55-year-old woman has Raynaud's phenomenon, tight skin of the fingers, telangiectasias, calcium deposits in the fingertips and heartburn from esophageal dysmotility. Which antibody is most associated with this presentation?
answer: The correct answer is A. This is CREST (calcinosis, Raynaud's, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia), the limited form of systemic sclerosis, associated with anti-centromere antibodies. Almost all SSc is ANA positive; anti-Scl-70 goes with diffuse disease and pulmonary fibrosis.

stem: A 62-year-old woman has 2 months of difficulty climbing stairs and lifting her arms. She has a violaceous rash on her upper eyelids and red papules over her knuckles. CK is markedly raised. Which association must be investigated?
answer: The correct answer is B. Inflammatory myositis causes proximal (shoulder and hip) weakness with raised CK. Dermatomyositis adds the heliotrope rash, Gottron papules and dilated nailfold capillaries, and in older adults it is associated with cancer, so screen for malignancy. Polymyositis has no rash or photosensitivity.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: 22 year old college student. New onset of: red rash on the cheeks (malar rash); maculopapular rash in the sun; fatigue; hands turning white in the cold (Raynaud's); weight loss; hair loss; stiff hands in the morning and swelling of knuckles. Her cousin has Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA).

stem: What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient and why?
answer: The correct answer is C. The case answers "Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)", and the lecture gives the why: a malar rash, a rash in the sun (photosensitivity), stiff swollen hands in the morning (possible inflammatory arthritis), hair loss (alopecia) and Raynaud's, with fatigue and weight loss. Alopecia and Raynaud's are common in SLE but are not classification criteria. Sjögren's syndrome (A) is dry eyes and mouth; dermatomyositis (B) is proximal weakness with a high CK, and its photosensitive rash is a V-neck or shawl rash with Gottron's papules over the knuckles, not a malar rash that spares the nasolabial folds; systemic sclerosis (D) is tight skin, dysphagia and fingertip ulcers.

preamble.title: The case, continued
preamble.html: The 22 year old college student with a malar rash, rash in the sun, Raynaud's, hair loss and stiff swollen knuckles. Her results: WBC 2.8 (normal 4-10) · Hgb 111 (normal 120-130) · Plt 43 (normal 150-350) · Creatinine 80 (normal 80-100) · Urine negative for protein and blood · Pregnancy test negative · ANA + 1/320 speckled · ENA: + for anti Smith (Sm) · Anti-DNA negative · C3 low, C4 low

stem: Does she have SLE? (the first line of the case is a recap written for this bank; the results and the question are copied from the lecture)

options.html: Yes: she meets at least 5 criteria
No: her anti-DNA antibody is negative
No: her kidneys are not involved
Not until a kidney biopsy is done

answer: The correct answer is A. The lecture: "Yes This patient has SLE." It counts: positive ANA; low white cells and platelets; positive anti-Smith and low complement (C3 and C4); malar rash; photosensitivity; possible inflammatory arthritis, "at least 5 criteria" where 4 of 11 are needed. A negative anti-DNA (B) does not exclude SLE: anti-Smith satisfies the same immunologic criterion. Kidney involvement (C) is one criterion among eleven, not a requirement, and nothing here calls for a biopsy (D).

preamble.html: Woman with rash in the sun, frequents sores in her mouth and nose, +ANA, +anti-DNA, blood and protein in urine?

stem: What is the likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is D. The lecture's answer: "SLE". A photosensitive rash, oral and nasal ulcers, a positive ANA with anti-DNA, and glomerulonephritis (blood and protein in the urine) are five of the eleven SLE criteria. Systemic sclerosis (A) would bring tight skin and dysphagia, Sjögren's (B) dry eyes and mouth with anti-Ro and anti-La, and dermatomyositis (C) proximal weakness with a high CK.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Woman with dry eyes and mouth severe enough to need to see her dentist regularly due to new repeated cavities, recurrent swelling of parotid glands, +ANA, +Ro, +La, recurrent leukocytoclastic vasculitis on shins

stem: What is the likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is B. The notes: "Sjogren's syndrome". Dry eyes and mouth (the sicca complex) with dental caries and parotid swelling, anti-Ro and anti-La, and leukocytoclastic vasculitis (purpura on the lower legs) are the Sjögren's picture in the notes. SLE (A) can carry anti-Ro but is not defined by sicca symptoms; systemic sclerosis (C) is tight skin and Raynaud's; dermatomyositis (D) is proximal weakness with a rash.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Woman with severe retrosternal dysphagia, tight skin on hands, arms and face, crackles on auscultation of lung bases, +ANA nucleolar pattern, +Scl70 (topoisomerase 1)

stem: What is the likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is A. The case answers: "Systemic sclerosis". Tight skin reaching the arms is diffuse cutaneous disease, and its antibodies are an ANA with a nucleolar pattern and anti-Scl-70, which "correlates with pulmonary fibrosis", the crackles at the lung bases (interstitial lung disease, "mostly at bases of lungs"). Dysphagia is common in scleroderma. Dermatomyositis (B) can cause swallowing trouble and lung disease, but through proximal weakness with anti-Jo-1, not tight skin; Sjögren's (C) and SLE (D) do not tighten the skin.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Woman or man with proximal muscle weakness, problems getting out of bed (due to core strength weakness), new Raynaud's, rash over knuckles, elevated CK

stem: What is the likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is C. The lecture: "DERMATOMYOSITIS". Proximal weakness with an elevated CK is inflammatory myositis, and the rash over the knuckles (Gottron's papules or sign) makes it dermatomyositis. Polymyositis (A) has the same weakness and CK but "no rash or photosensitivity". The SLE photosensitive rash (B) is not a knuckle rash, and systemic sclerosis (D) brings Raynaud's but not a myopathy with a rash.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mrs. Tran's painful knee: 52 years old, female. History of type 2 diabetes. Knee pain since age 45, now getting worse and more frequent. Pain is limiting her from daily walks and using the stairs. Stiffness in the knee in the morning for 5 minutes after waking. Appears well, but walking with a slight antalgic gait. On examination, the right knee is slightly swollen but feels cool. Tender to palpation along the joint line. Crepitus is noted on passive flexion.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is B. The notes: "Mrs. Tran has chronic monoarthritis caused by knee OA." Pain brought on by activity (walks, stairs), morning stiffness under 30 minutes (usually under 5), and a tender joint with a cool effusion are the OA presentation, with no red flags. OA is a clinical diagnosis. Infection (A) gives a warm or hot joint. Rheumatoid arthritis (C) is an inflammatory polyarthritis, and chronic crystal arthritis (D) is the fourth item on the differential after "osteoarthritis" three times.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Ms. Markus' intermittent knee pain: 36 years old, female soccer star. No medical problems, but tore ACL in a soccer match at age 23. Pain only with running for 5 years, now increasing swelling. Stiffness in the knee in the morning for 5 minutes after waking. No red flags for other types of arthritis.

stem: Does Ms. Markus have knee OA? (stem copied from the lecture; options written for this bank)

options.html: No, she is too young to have osteoarthritis
No, osteoarthritis needs X-ray changes first
No, her pain is intermittent, not daily

answer: The correct answer is D. The lecture: "Yes, she has post-traumatic knee OA - Not too young for that!" Her risk of needing a knee replacement by age 55 is over 50%. Post-traumatic OA after an ACL or meniscus tear is secondary OA, and most symptomatic knee OA starts between 35 and 55 (A). OA is a clinical diagnosis; X-ray changes alone do not diagnose it (B). Her symptoms are activity-related with brief morning stiffness and no red flags, the OA pattern (C).

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mr. Liebowitz' progressive knee pain and stiffness: 68 male with chronic left knee pain and stiffness, worse after activity, with occasional "flare ups" of knee pain and swelling. Medical history includes dyslipidemia, chronic renal failure, and left total hip arthroplasty for hip OA (2001). Medications include atorvastatin 40 mg daily. Pain and stiffness has progressed to such an extent that he moved out of his 2-storey house into a retirement home. No red flags for other causes of arthritis. Left knee exam demonstrates varus knee alignment. Tenderness and crepitus on the knee examination and limitation in passive left knee flexion due to pain. X-ray: joint space narrowing and osteophytes.

stem: Which of the following best describes his diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is C. The lecture: "Mr. Liebowitz has late stage knee OA." The X-ray shows joint space narrowing and osteophytes, staged on the early / late / end-stage scale. End-stage (B) is where he is two years later, with bone-on-bone contact, a cane and symptoms uncontrolled despite every non-surgical treatment. There are no red flags for other causes of arthritis (D).

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mr. Liebowitz, above: late stage left knee OA, chronic renal failure, varus alignment.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate plan? (the lecture gives "You recommend he try" without posing a question; stem written for this bank)

options.html: Neuromuscular physiotherapy, OT education, topical NSAID
Regular oral naproxen, with tramadol for any breakthrough pain
Arthroscopic debridement of the knee with a meniscectomy
Passive therapy: ultrasound, TENS and acupuncture sessions

answer: The correct answer is A. The lecture: physiotherapy for neuromuscular strength and stability training for at least 3 months, OT to educate on safe movements, consider topical NSAIDs BID to TID (avoid oral NSAIDs for chronic renal failure), a corticosteroid injection if refractory, and an SNRI trial for 2-3 months if still refractory. Oral NSAIDs are out with his kidneys, and opioids including tramadol are generally avoided (risks > benefit) (B). Knee arthroscopy has strong level 1 evidence of no meaningful benefit (C). Passive therapies are not shown to be beneficial (D).

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mr. Liebowitz, 2 years later, returns with worse pain and now is using a cane. His x-rays show end-stage damage with severe joint space narrowing (bone on bone contact). He has not had adequate control of his symptoms or been able to maintain his physical function despite appropriate physical exercise therapy, education, topical, oral, and injectable medical therapies.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step? (the lecture reveals the referral and the evidence without posing a question; stem written for this bank)

options.html: A repeat corticosteroid injection every month
Start a long-acting opioid for the pain

answer: The correct answer is B. In the lecture he asks for an orthopedic consultation for left knee arthroplasty, and joint replacement is RECOMMENDED, with strong level 1 evidence of benefit over non-surgical care alone; it is the salvage procedure for end-stage disease with unacceptable symptoms. Arthroscopy (A) is NOT RECOMMENDED, with strong evidence of no meaningful benefit. Steroid injections (C) give only short-term relief, and opioids (D) are generally avoided.

preamble.title: The cases
preamble.html:
Case 1. 5 year old girl previously well. Presents with a 3 month history of bilateral knee swelling and morning limp. She is otherwise systemically well. O/E there are multiple active joints: bilateral knees, left wrist, many small joints of the hands.

Case 2. 3 year old boy previously well. Presents with: 3 months of intermittent fevers; 2 months of joint pain and swelling involving both knees and ankles; several episodes of faint rash, lasting up to a few hours. O/E he appears fatigued, pale; splenomegaly; effusions of both knees and ankles.

stem: Do these patients have JIA?

options.html: Only Case 1: Case 2's fevers rule out JIA
Only Case 2: Case 1 has too many joints
Neither: both have lasted too short a time
Both fit, once other causes are excluded

answer: The answer is D, reasoned from the lecture; the lecture asks the question and says "We will return to this case at the end", but never states an answer. The lecture's criteria are onset under 16, arthritis in one or more joints, duration over 6 weeks, and other causes excluded. Case 1 (age 5, 3 months) and Case 2 (age 3, 2 months of joint swelling) both meet the first three, and JIA is "a diagnosis of exclusion", so both fit once other causes are ruled out. Fever does not rule JIA out (A): high spiking fevers define systemic JIA, which is often first thought to be infection or leukemia, so those must be excluded. No joint count is too many (B): one or more joints qualifies, and 5 or more is polyarticular JIA. Both have lasted well over the 6 weeks the criteria need (C).

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: 5 year old girl previously well. Presents with a 3 month history of bilateral knee swelling and morning limp. She is otherwise systemically well. O/E there are multiple active joints: bilateral knees, left wrist, many small joints of the hands.

stem: If this is JIA, what is the most likely subtype?
answer: The answer is B, reasoned from the lecture; the session poses the question without an answer. Both knees, the left wrist and many small joints of the hands are 5 or more joints, which is polyarticular JIA (the notes: "joint pain and swelling in 5 or more joints during the first 6 months"); a younger child with polyarthritis fits the rheumatoid factor-negative group, though the case gives no rheumatoid factor result here. Oligoarticular JIA (A) is 4 or fewer joints. Systemic JIA (C) needs high spiking fevers and rash, and she is systemically well. Enthesitis-related arthritis (D) is more common in boys, usually over 10, with enthesitis and sacroiliitis.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: 5 year old girl previously well. Presents with a 3 month history of bilateral knee swelling and morning limp. She is otherwise systemically well. O/E there are multiple active joints: bilateral knees, left wrist, many small joints of the hands.

stem: As this child's primary care provider, what will your next steps in management be?

options.html: Order an ANA, and refer to rheumatology only if it comes back positive
Start oral prednisone and book an eye exam in 12 months
Order initial tests, start an NSAID, refer to rheumatology and eyes
Start methotrexate, then refer to rheumatology if she fails it

answer: The answer is C, reasoned from the lecture's take-home message, since the lecture poses the question without answering it: "The initial management often includes ordering preliminary investigations, starting NSAID therapy and referring to Rheumatology and Optometry/Ophthalmology." The ANA does not decide the referral (A): it is "used to prognosticate risk of uveitis, NOT to diagnose JIA". Oral steroids are a bridge in polyarticular disease, not the first step, and a young child with polyarthritis is screened for uveitis every 3 to 6 months, not yearly (B). Methotrexate is a second-line agent started in rheumatology care (D).

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: 3 year old boy previously well. Presents with: 3 months of intermittent fevers; 2 months of joint pain and swelling involving both knees and ankles; several episodes of faint rash, lasting up to a few hours. O/E he appears fatigued, pale; splenomegaly; effusions of both knees and ankles.

stem: If this is JIA, what is the most likely subtype?
answer: The answer is A, reasoned from the lecture; the lecture poses the question without an answer. Fevers, a faint rash that comes and goes ("evanescent"), splenomegaly (organomegaly) and arthritis are the systemic JIA picture (high spiking fevers, inflammatory arthritis, rash), which affects boys and girls equally at any age. Four joints would make it oligoarticular (B) and 5 or more polyarticular (D), but neither explains the fever, rash or spleen. Psoriatic JIA (C) needs a family history of psoriasis, nail pitting, onycholysis or dactylitis.

stem: What is one serious complication of this particular subtype of JIA?
answer: The answer is D, reasoned from the lecture; the lecture poses the question without an answer. Systemic JIA is "the most serious and potentially life threatening subtype", and the summary names its unique consideration: "macrophage activation syndrome in the context of SJIA". Ankylosing spondylitis (A) develops in 30% of enthesitis-related arthritis. Silent uveitis (B) is the risk of oligo- and polyarticular JIA; in the screening table systemic JIA has the longest interval, every 12 months. Micrognathia (C) is a local growth disturbance any subtype can cause, not the complication particular to systemic JIA.

stem: As this child's primary care provider, what will your next steps in management be?

options.html: Start an IL-1 blocker now, before any blood work is drawn
Order initial tests, start an NSAID, refer to rheumatology and eyes
Treat as septic arthritis and wait for the fever to settle first
Reassure the family; the faint rash and fevers point to a passing virus

answer: The answer is B, reasoned from the lecture's take-home points, since the lecture poses the question without answering it: "The initial management often includes ordering preliminary investigations, starting NSAID therapy and referring to Rheumatology and Optometry/Ophthalmology." The preliminary bloods matter more than usual here, because systemic JIA is "often thought to have an infection or leukemia" and those have to be excluded. Interleukin-1 blockade (A) is specialist treatment for fever and systemic features that persist on systemic steroids. Three months of fever, two of joint swelling and a big spleen are not a passing virus (D), and the lecture gives no reason to treat this as septic arthritis (C).

lectureMeta: Workbook Q19-Q22, Q32, Q50, Q67. Tests [[05 - Fracture Radiology]], [[07 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A comminuted fracture is a:

options.html: Fracture involving the flare of a long bone
Fracture involving more than two fragments

answer:
The correct answer is D. Comminuted = more than two fragments. The distractors are the other descriptors:

  • A → diaphyseal fracture
  • B → metaphyseal fracture ("the flare")
  • C → intra-articular fracture

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q19-Q22, Q32, Q50, Q67. Tests [[05 - Fracture Radiology]], [[07 - Fracture Management]].
stem: Complete the following statement: A _____ fracture does not involve external environmental contamination and has _____ outcomes whereas a _____ fracture involves contamination of soft tissues and has _____ outcomes.
answer:
The correct answer is B. Closed → better; open → poorer.

From Fracture Management and Fracture Radiology. An open (compound) fracture exposes the bone or fracture hematoma to the external environment through a break in the skin, so it is contaminated by definition. The lecture lists its cost: ↑ infection, non-union, delayed union and incomplete recovery, worst after high-energy trauma. That is why management aims to convert an unstable, contaminated wound into a stable, clean one - early antibiotics and tetanus, debridement and irrigation, early closure. A closed fracture keeps the soft-tissue envelope intact and does better.

  • A gets the outcomes backwards.
  • C, D swap the definitions: it is the open fracture that is contaminated.

Any wound near a fracture, even a distant one, counts as open until proven otherwise.
