weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q78-Q79, Q82-Q84. Tests [[05 - Fracture Radiology]], [[07 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A 25-year-old man presents to the emergency department after falling off his skateboard onto his outstretched right hand. He reports immediate pain and swelling in the wrist and is unable to move his hand. On physical exam, there is tenderness to palpation over the anatomical snuffbox and decreased sensation over the radial aspect of the hand. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is A. FOOSH injuries are a common cause of wrist fractures, with the scaphoid the most commonly fractured bone in the wrist. The anatomical snuffbox is on the radial side of the wrist and contains the scaphoid; snuffbox tenderness is the classic finding, and patients may also have decreased sensation over the radial aspect of the hand from injury to the superficial radial nerve.

The distractors, each with its own signature:

  • Colles fracture — distal radius with dorsal displacement, typically older patients with osteoporosis (see Q84)
  • Radial head fracture — at the elbow; adults who FOOSH with an extended elbow
  • Distal radius fracture — common, but does not involve the anatomical snuffbox

See scaphoid fracture.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q78-Q79, Q82-Q84. Tests [[05 - Fracture Radiology]], [[07 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A 35-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after a fall on her outstretched hand. She reports immediate pain and swelling in the wrist and is unable to move her hand. X-rays are negative for fracture, but there is tenderness to palpation over the anatomic snuffbox and the patient is unable to grip objects. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.html: Place the wrist in a cast for 6 weeks
Perform a CT scan of the wrist
Order an MRI of the wrist

answer:
The correct answer is D. A negative x-ray does not rule out a scaphoid fracture — scaphoid fractures may not be visible on initial films. With high clinical suspicion, order an MRI, which is the imaging modality of choice for diagnosing them.

Why the rest fail: A — casting for 6 weeks without proper diagnosis may lead to further complications. B — a repeat x-ray in 1 week may still not show the fracture. C — CT shows better detail than plain film, but MRI is the modality of choice.

Why this matters: a scaphoid fracture is a serious injury and can lead to avascular necrosis of the bone if left untreated — the same blood-supply logic as Q13.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q78-Q79, Q82-Q84. Tests [[05 - Fracture Radiology]], [[07 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A 7-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after falling off his bike and injuring his forearm. X-rays reveal an incomplete fracture of the radius with evidence of cortical thickening on the convex side of the bone, and no significant displacement or angulation. Which of the following types of fractures is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is E. Incomplete fracture with cortical thickening on the convex side is characteristic of a greenstick fracture. These are common in children because of the pliability of their bones, and typically occur in long bones when a bending force is applied.

The distractors:

  • Colles fracture — distal radius fracture in older adults who FOOSH
  • Monteggia fracture — fracture of the proximal ulna with dislocation of the radial head
  • Buckle fracture — an incomplete fracture with bulging of the cortex on one side due to compression
  • Torus fracture — another term for a buckle fracture, which is why C and D cannot both be the single best answer

lectureMeta: Workbook Q78-Q79, Q82-Q84. Tests [[05 - Fracture Radiology]], [[07 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A 28-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a history of falling onto his outstretched arm during a football game. He complains of severe pain in his left shoulder and inability to move it. On examination, his left arm is held in adduction and internal rotation. X-ray reveals a dislocated humeral head posterior to the glenoid. What is the most common cause of posterior shoulder dislocations?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Trauma is the most common cause of posterior shoulder dislocations, accounting for approximately 75-90% of cases.

Seizures and electric shock can also cause posterior dislocations — they are the classically taught associations — but they are much less common, which is the trap this question sets. A rotator cuff tear is not a cause of posterior dislocation.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q78-Q79, Q82-Q84. Tests [[05 - Fracture Radiology]], [[07 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A 55-year-old female presents to the emergency department after falling on her outstretched hand. She complains of wrist pain and deformity. On examination, her wrist is swollen and tender, and there is an obvious dorsal angulation of the distal radius. X-ray reveals a fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement. What is the name of this fracture?
answer:
The answer is D — Colles fracture.

From Colles fracture and Smith's fracture. Two discriminators settle every distal-forearm eponym: the mechanism and the direction of the distal fragment. A Colles fracture is the FOOSH (fall onto outstretched hand) injury with dorsal angulation of the distal radius - exactly this stem, in the older patient the workbook's own Q78 describes.

  • A fails: Smith's fracture is the reverse - volar displacement, from a fall on a flexed wrist or a blow to the dorsum.
  • B fails: Monteggia is a proximal ulna fracture with radial head dislocation - the elbow, not the wrist (Q82).
  • C fails: Barton is an intra-articular rim fracture of the distal radius with carpal subluxation; nothing here says intra-articular.

flags.title: No answer in the workbook
flags.html:
The key stops at Q83; there is no entry for Q84. The answer above is reasoned, but it is well supported by the workbook's own text elsewhere: Q78's explanation defines a Colles fracture as "a fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement of the wrist... typically seen in older patients with osteoporosis" — exactly this stem.

The distractors: Smith fracture is the reverse (distal radius with volar/palmar displacement); Monteggia is proximal ulna + radial head dislocation (per Q82); Barton is an intra-articular distal radius fracture with carpal subluxation.

The etiology like calcaneovarus and metatarsus adductus is related to intrauterine positioning rather than genetics
This condition appears to be more prevalent among females
All of the above are correct

answer:
The correct answer is A. That is the correct description of the natural history of congenital talipes equinovarus.

B is the substantive error: there are many etiological theories for clubfoot — arrested embryologic development, neurologic causes, muscular fibrosis — and there is some relationship with polygenic multifactorial inheritance, so it cannot be attributed to intrauterine positioning alone the way calcaneovarus and metatarsus adductus can.

stem: In the analysis and description of curvature in a scoliosis patient requires the following except:

options.html: Ruling out any anatomical abnormalities (i.e. from trauma or tumours)
All of the above are required

answer:
The correct answer is F — all of the above are required. What each term means when describing a scoliosis curve:

  • Location — whether the vertex of the curve is cervical, thoracic or lumbar
  • Spinal level — the actual levels the curvature spans
  • Direction — whether the concavity points right or left
  • Magnitude — the number of degrees
  • Abnormalities — is there a fracture cause or tumour driving the curvature that could be addressed

stem: Which of the following are not a risk factor for further progression of scoliosis.

options.html: Onset at an older physiologic age
Thoracic are at greater risk than lumbar
Larger curves are at greater risk than smaller curves

answer: The correct answer is A. Patients who are physiologically older have less skeletal bone growth remaining, and therefore less potential for progression of scoliosis through asymmetric bone growth. Progression risk tracks remaining growth — so younger onset is the risk, not older.

stem: A 16-year-old patient comes to you with complaints of a rib hump that was noticed during a physiotherapy session for a shoulder injury she had. You complete a neurological examination which is normal as well as characterize her spinal curvature. You note a Right Thoracic curve from level T7-T12 with a 34-degree curve. The most appropriate treatment would be:

options.html: Follow the person with annual radiologic examination to assess progression

answer: The correct answer is C. Bracing. Patients with 30-40 degrees of curve are recommended to have bracing treatment, with the main goal of preventing further progression (not of correcting the existing curve). Her 34° falls squarely in that band. See scoliosis.

stem: A 13-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with hip pain and an abnormal gait. Imaging reveals a femoral head displacement, which was not initially evident on plain radiographs. The patient has a BMI of 35, and is undergoing hormonal therapy for a pre-existing medical condition. Which of the following management options is most appropriate for this patient?

options.html: Observation and follow-up imaging in 4 weeks
Non-weight bearing with crutches and physical therapy
Surgical reduction and internal fixation of the hip
Encourage weight loss and activity modification

answer:
The correct answer is C. This is SCFE, and the stem's two risk factors — high BMI and hormonal therapy — are what flag it.

Surgical reduction and internal fixation is typically required for moderate to severe cases, to prevent further displacement and degenerative arthritis. B may be appropriate for some cases, and A for mild ones — but the pain and abnormal gait here suggest a moderate to severe case. D is beneficial for overall health and future prevention but is not sufficient treatment for an acute SCFE.

stem: A 4-year-old girl presents to the clinic with a history of frequent falls and difficulty with balance. She also complains of leg pain at night that is relieved by rubbing. On physical exam, she has a waddling gait and is unable to stand on one leg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is A. Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (LCPD) is a non-traumatic condition of the hip joint in children, occurring when blood flow to the femoral head is interrupted, leading to bone death and subsequent deformation.

Symptoms: hip or groin pain, limping, difficulty with mobility. Nighttime pain relieved by rubbing is a classic feature. Children may have a waddling gait and be unable to stand on one leg.

DDH, JIA, osteogenesis imperfecta and SCFE can present similarly — the history and exam here are what favour LCPD. Note the age contrast with Q80: LCPD in a 4-year-old, SCFE in a 13-year-old.

stem: In which of the following cases is ordering an ANA indicated? Choose 1

options.html: A family doctor is unsure if a patient has an autoimmune disorder and the patient had a negative ANA result last year (no new symptoms).
A rheumatologist wants to follow a SLE patient’s progress/response to treatment.
A patient presents to the ER with delirium, acute pericarditis, fever, alopecia, and proteinuria.
A patient is presenting with swollen and achy knees that are stiff (<30 min every morning), prone to night pain, and have a reduced ROM.

answer: The correct answer is C. In answer C, the patient actually fulfills multiple clinical domains for SLE. Since an autoimmune CTD is suspected, ANA can be ordered. ANA is not ordered if there was a negative ANA in the past. It is also not ordered to follow a patient. Case D describes a patient with osteoarthritis (not inflammatory = no ANA needed).

stem: A 63 y.o Finnish patient presents to the ER with sudden painless vision loss, an awful headache, pain with chewing, and pain with laying his head on their pillow at night. He also mentions pain in his shoulders and hips and classic B symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats)! What should the next steps be? Choose 3

options.html: Consult oncology urgently due to risk of intracranial malignancy
Consult ophthalmology for a temporal artery biopsy

answer: The correct answer is A, E, F. This patient has giant cell arteritis. Low-dose prednisone is only reserved for cases where other options don’t work or there are difficulty discontinuing steroids. Medium-dose prednisone is for RA flares, polymyalgia rheumatica and acute gout flare. Remember to not wait for ESR/CRP results and to start high dose corticosteroids immediately! Patients who are of Northern European descent (e.g. Finnish in this case) are at greater risk of giant cell arteritis. Intracranial malignancies need to be ruled out but doesn’t require oncology consult.

stem: Which of the following is false?

options.html: Prior to diagnosing primary vasculitis, serum protein electrophoresis, urine toxicology screens, sputum cultures, Hep B+C serology, and HIV testing must be taken.
Common signs of primary vasculitis includes ecchymosis, intracranial hemorrhages, cranial nerve neuropathies, and concurrent infections.
Giant cell arteritis cannot affect people who are 49 years old or younger.
A patient with ANCA vasculitis can still have a negative ANCA.
Patients with primary vasculitis need to have the following investigations to check for organ involvement: ALT, albumin, Cr, urinalysis, chest x-ray.
Vasculitis involves blood vessel thickening from inflammation and a resulting turbulent blood flow.

answer: The correct answer is B. Common signs of vasculitis are actually petechial/purpural rashes and B-symptoms (infections must actually be ruled out to make a diagnosis of primary vasculitis). Clots, occlusions/ischemia and aneurysms are more of a concern than bleeding manifestations in vasculitis. A is true because infection and underlying malignancy/drugs must be ruled out.

stem:
Match the complication (a,b,c,d,e) to the condition (i, ii, iii, iv). Warning: there may be repeats (e.g. one condition has 1+ complications)

  1. SLE
  2. Scleroderma
  3. inflammatory myositis
  4. Sjogren’s
answer:
The correct answer is A. iii, B - iv, C - i, D - i & ii, E - ii

From 09 - Connective Tissue Disorders. Each complication is a signature of one disease:

  • A → iii (myositis): pharyngeal and cardiac muscle involvement (aspiration, arrhythmia) plus the paraneoplastic link of dermatomyositis in the elderly.
  • B → iv (Sjogren's): ↑ risk of non-Hodgkin, specifically MALT lymphoma.
  • C → i (SLE): 50x cardiovascular risk; accelerated atherosclerosis is the commonest cause of death, worsened by steroids.
  • D → ii (scleroderma): significant ILD in ~15%, tracked by anti-Scl-70.
  • E → ii (scleroderma): renal crisis in diffuse disease (RNA-polymerase), now rarer thanks to ACE inhibitors.

flags.title: The key looks wrong on D
flags.html: The key maps interstitial lung disease to SLE and scleroderma. 09 - Connective Tissue Disorders and its embedded disease notes attach ILD to scleroderma, myositis (anti-Jo1) and Sjogren's; the SLE lung section lists pleuritis and pulmonary capillaritis, not ILD. Scleroderma is the safe answer for D; SLE is not supported by the notes.

stem: Match the common presentation to the pediatric condition.
answer:
The pairings:

PresentationPediatric condition
A child (between 3-10 y.o) who was sick with a URTI about a week ago now has sudden unilateral hip pain and their hip is held in slight FABER positionTransient synovitis
An adolescent athlete (8-14 y.o female, 10-15 y.o male) has a painful bump over their tibial tuberosity and xray shows a teardrop sign.Osgood-Schlatter
An obese adolescent (~ 12 y.o female, 14 y.o male) has gradual left hip pain that refers to the knee, antalgic gait, and can’t weight bearSlipped capital femoral epiphysis
A child (between 4-8 y.o) who has a low body weight and protein S/C deficiency has gradual vague hip pain and stiffness and limb-length discrepancyLegg-Calve-Perthes

From 09 - Child with a Limp and 04 - Pediatric Orthopedics. Age plus one hallmark sorts each:

  • Transient synovitis: ages 3-10, a viral URTI 7-10 days earlier, sudden unilateral hip pain, the hip held flexed, abducted and externally rotated, afebrile.
  • Osgood-Schlatter: traction apophysitis at the tibial tuberosity in active 8-14 (F) / 10-15 (M) year olds; x-ray shows the "teardrop" sign.
  • SCFE: adolescent, gradual hip pain referred to the knee, left more often than right, painful weight-bearing.
  • Legg-Calve-Perthes: ages 4-8, low birth weight, gradual vague hip pain, stiffness and limb-length discrepancy from femoral-head osteonecrosis.

The stem's protein S/C deficiency is not in the note; its risk factors are family history, low birth weight and second-hand smoke.

stem: Over the phone, your friend Marnie tells you that she is sad because her manicurist made mean comments about her nails. stem: Which of the following cases likely has polymyalgia rheumatica?

options.html: A 64 y.o patient who has a history of giant cell arteritis presents with new weight loss and also pain in shoulder and hip.
A 43 y.o male presenting with pain and stiffness in the shoulder and hip girdles with profound morning stiffness and fatigue.
A 56 y.o febrile female presenting with pain in just her left shoulder, which is also warm and swollen.

A 73 y.o patient with long-standing pain in hip (which is not stiff), worse with activity. Her shoulder muscles has weakness but no pain. They sadly have not responded to prednisone that you previously prescribed.

answer: The correct answer is A. giant cell arteritis often occurs with polymyalgia rheumatica. B is not correct because polymyalgia rheumatica only affects people older than 50. C is likely septic arthritis (bacterial monoarthritis). D is likely hip osteoarthritis and shoulder myositis. Polymyalgia rheumatica won’t have muscle weakness and should respond dramatically to prednisone.

stem: Your 45 year old male patient comes in for regular blood work. Results show that he has elevated uric acid. What are your next steps? Choose the best answer.

options.html: Advise him to start eating more seafood

answer: The correct answer is C. Hyperuricemia does not necessarily mean gout. In this case, this patient does not have any symptoms of gout (i.e., swollen joint, red, painful). Therefore, doing further investigations and/or treatment is unnecessary. Furthermore, if you patient has gout, you should advise them to decrease the amount of seafood in their diet; and we typically do not prescribe allopurinol right away (unless it is debilitating to their life), and especially not during the gout attack. Lastly, gout is more commonly found on 1st MTP joint (big toe), not on the knee (CPPD more commonly found in knee).

stem: Which of the following are not appropriate treatment plan for CPPD?
answer:
The correct answer is A. Colchicine is used to treat gout.

From 04 - Acute Monoarthritis and the MSK summary notes. An acute pseudogout (CPPD) attack is treated like an acute gout attack: NSAIDs (indomethacin), colchicine, or steroids (intra-articular or oral prednisone). What does not carry over from gout is urate lowering (allopurinol), which is for gout only.

  • A (colchicine) is on the notes' acute-attack list for pseudogout.
  • B, D are both listed: IA injection and a short oral prednisone taper.
  • C is an NSAID; a COXIB belongs to the same class as the indomethacin in the notes.

So on the notes, every option is an appropriate treatment for CPPD.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key says colchicine is inappropriate because it is a gout drug. The MSK summary notes list colchicine for acute pseudogout attacks, and the Schulich MSK review notes it on the slide (SR slide 115), although the embedded pseudogout note leaves it out. Colchicine is used in CPPD, so no option here is clearly inappropriate. The key's distinction is allopurinol, not colchicine.

stem: Your 65 year old patient has early stage Osteoarthritis. She strongly asks you if she could get a joint replacement surgery. What would be your response?

options.html: No - we should perform knee arthroscopy.
No - treatment for early stage OA is monitoring & reassurance with absolutely no intervention

No - joint replacement surgeries are advised on end-stage OA patients who have tried every other non-invasive methods and still have failed to improve. We can instead try other methods like Tai-Chi and physiotherapy first.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 06 - Osteoarthritis. OA treatment is staged first (early, late, end stage), then goes in order: non-pharmacologic, pharmacologic, surgical. Arthroplasty is a salvage procedure for end-stage disease no longer controlled by other therapies, and early OA starts with active, neuromuscular-control exercise (Tai Chi is the lecture's example), weight loss and assistive devices.

  • A fails: early-stage disease is not an indication for replacement.
  • B fails: the notes say only arthroplasty has real benefit; arthroscopy is not recommended.
  • C fails: early OA is actively treated (exercise, weight management, topical NSAIDs), not just watched.

stem: Which of the following should we try to avoid for medical treatment of early-middle stage OA?
answer:
The correct answer is E. We should generally avoid tramadol (opioid).

From 06 - Osteoarthritis. The OA drug list marks opioids "generally avoid": tramadol has some evidence but its risks have to be weighed, and opioids sit in the Not recommended box. 03 - Rheumatology Treatments adds why: opioids do nothing for inflammation and bring cognitive impairment, constipation and dependence.

  • A fails: topical and oral NSAIDs are first-line approved OA treatments (topical is inconclusive only for the hip).
  • C fails: an intra-articular steroid injection is listed for short-term relief.
  • D fails: duloxetine is the SNRI to try when other therapies fail.
  • B (oral prednisone) is not on the OA list at all, but it is not what the lecture flags to avoid.

flags.title: B is not an OA treatment either
flags.html: 06 - Osteoarthritis lists only intra-articular steroids; systemic prednisone is a rheumatology drug for inflammatory disease (03 - Rheumatology Treatments). The key's E is the option the notes explicitly say to avoid, but do not read B as endorsed for OA.

stem: Which of the following affects Sacroiliac joints?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

From 07 - Approach to Polyarthritis. The lecture's rule is flat: whenever the sacroiliac joint is involved, think seronegative spondyloarthropathy (ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic, IBD-associated, reactive). Axial disease with asymmetric large peripheral joints is their pattern, and inflammatory back pain (better with movement, worse in the second half of the night) goes with it.

  • A, B fail: CTD arthritis and RA are symmetric small- and large-joint peripheral diseases.
  • D fails: OA targets weight-bearing joints, the 1st CMC and DIPs; its spine disease is facet OA, not sacroiliitis.

stem: Which of the following favour small joints in the hand and feet, and spares distal phalangeal joints?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 07 - Approach to Polyarthritis. The distribution table is the discriminator: MCP joints point to RA, and the DIP joints are usually SPARED in RA and other connective tissue diseases. Symmetric small- and large-joint involvement completes the RA pattern.

  • A fails: OA is one of the diseases that does hit the DIPs (with the 1st CMC).
  • B fails: seronegative disease is axial (SI joints, spine) with asymmetric large joints, and psoriatic arthritis also targets the DIPs.
  • C fails: infection is typically a single hot joint, not a symmetric small-joint pattern.

stem: What type of JIA is not commonly associated with asymptomatic uveitis?
answer: The correct answer is C. In all other types of JIA, uveitis is a serious yet asymptomatic complication that can potentially lead to blindness ( essential that children get regular screening done). However, in enthesitis related JIA, uveitis is markedly painful (aka symptomatic) and red!

stem: A knee aspirate from a febrile patient is cloudy, with a white cell count of 80,000 cells/mm³. What does this count most strongly suggest?
answer: The correct answer is E. Synovial white cell count: <2,000 non-inflammatory (e.g., OA); ≥2,000 inflammatory; ≥50,000 suggests septic arthritis. Always send culture/gram stain and crystals as well.

stem: How would you treat this? 65 year-old woman with acute-onset pain in pelvic and shoulder girdles bilaterally. ESR 50 mm/hr

options.html: Prednisone ~1 mg/kg daily, then a slow taper
Prednisone 15-20 mg daily, then a slow taper
IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily x 3 days
Prednisone 25 mg daily x 3 days, then taper

answer: The correct answer is B. The notes on polymyalgia rheumatica: it "typically does not require high-dose prednisone"; the standard dose is 15-20 mg daily, then a rapid taper to 10 mg, then a slow taper by 1 mg every 4 weeks until off. It is self-limited (6 months to 2 years). A (high dose) is needed only if giant cell arteritis is also present (~15%), to decrease the risk of blindness. C (pulse steroids) is for an emergency such as giant cell arteritis with vision involvement. D is the short acute gout course.

flags.title: The notes give two schedules
flags.html: One part of the notes says 15-20 mg daily x 4 weeks then taper quickly to 10 mg; the polymyalgia rheumatica section says x 2 weeks then a rapid taper to 10 mg "weekly" over a couple of weeks. Both continue with 1 mg every 4 weeks. The options avoid the duration.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: 45 year old man with a 6 week history of a painful, non-blancheable rash on his legs. Over this time period, he has felt generally unwell with significant fatigue. He has pain and swelling in his ankles bilaterally. The rash is purpura.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is B. The lecture reveals it on its classification chart: cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis is "Diagnosis of case 1", a small vessel vasculitis that "can occur on its own or be a manifestation of other vasculitis types". The lecture frames the rash's differential as "coagulopathy or vasculitis". Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (A) is an ANCA-associated vasculitis whose common features are sinonasal, eye, lung and kidney disease, none of which he has. Polyarteritis nodosa (C) is a medium vessel vasculitis. Henoch-Schönlein purpura (D) is a small vessel vasculitis with purpura too, but the lecture marks it as one of the two most common in children. The module carries this same man forward, where hepatitis C turns out to be the cause (module Q161-162).

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html:
75 year old female with prior history of high blood pressure treated with a small dose of hydrochlorothiazide. Patient developed a right-sided temporal headaches that quickly got worse over 1 week. She has never had a headache like this before. She noticed that it hurt to brush her hair. She was having trouble eating because of jaw pain. 2 months ago she complained of shoulder and hip pain and stiffness worse in the morning. She was very fatigued and had lost same weight.

Laboratory investigations: Hemoglobin 99 (115-145) · WBC normal · Platelets normal · ESR 70 mm/hr (normal < 20) · CRP 50 (normal <5)

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is D. The case: "The family doctor was concerned about giant cell arteritis." She is over 50 with a new headache unlike any before, scalp tenderness (it hurt to brush her hair), jaw claudication, polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms (shoulder and hip pain and stiffness, worse in the morning), weight loss and fatigue, with anemia and a high ESR and CRP. All three distractors are on the notes' differential of a cranial presentation: temporomandibular arthritis (A) would explain jaw pain but not the scalp tenderness, the girdle stiffness or the inflammatory markers; a migraine (B) does not start for the first time at 75 with raised markers; sinusitis (C) does not cause jaw claudication or limb girdle stiffness.

preamble.title: The case, continued
preamble.html: The 75 year old woman with a new right temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain on eating, morning shoulder and hip stiffness, and an ESR of 70 and CRP of 50. Her family doctor is concerned about giant cell arteritis.

stem: What is the most appropriate next step? (stem written for the lecture's answer; the lecture poses no question)

options.html: Prescribe prednisone today, then refer to rheumatology
Book a biopsy; start prednisone only if it is positive
Repeat the ESR and CRP in 2 weeks, then decide on treatment
Start prednisone 15 mg daily and review in 2 weeks

answer: The correct answer is A. The lecture: "The patient was given a prescription that day for 50 mg daily of prednisone. A referral to Rheumatology was made. The patient felt 100% better after 5 days of prednisone." The lecture gives the rule: as soon as GCA is suspected, measure the ESR and CRP and start prednisone 1 mg/kg (max 60 mg daily) once the blood is drawn, and do not wait for results; then protect against steroid side effects (proton pump inhibitor, calcium and vitamin D, bisphosphonate) and arrange a temporal artery biopsy or Doppler ultrasound. Waiting for a biopsy (B) or for repeat markers (C) risks vision loss, which in 15-20% is permanent; a negative biopsy would not rule GCA out anyway, since 50-70% are negative from skip lesions. 15-20 mg (D) is the polymyalgia rheumatica dose, and polymyalgia with GCA needs high-dose prednisone "to decrease the risk of blindness" (Rheumatology Treatments, steroids lecture).

preamble.title: The case - purpura and ankle swelling
preamble.html:
The case. 45 year old man with a 6 week history of a painful, non-blancheable rash on his legs. Over this time period, he has felt generally unwell with significant fatigue. He has pain and swelling in his ankles bilaterally. The rash has the appearance of purpura. Prior to developing the rash, the patient felt well. He has no past medical history and avoids going to see the doctor. He works in sales and is married with two children aged 3 and 5. He has a family history of heart disease in his father; no family history of cancer or rheumatologic disease. He denies any recent travel outside of Canada. He drinks 2-3 alcoholic beverages daily and smokes a pack-a-day of cigarettes. He uses marijuana recreationally once a month. He denies any other drug use but did use i.v. drugs 10 years ago. He has several tattoos. He denies any unprotected sex other than with his wife.

Regarding his current symptoms, these are getting worse over the last week. The bilateral ankle pain is worse in the morning and associated with 2 hours of stiffness. He has been using ibuprofen 800 mg, 3 times daily for the pain in his legs. He did not find that acetaminophen helped his symptoms and he has not been using it. He does not take any other medications, vitamins or herbals. He denies any history of red, painful eyes, headaches, sinus congestion or epistaxis. He has no hearing problems. He denies dyspnea, cough or chest pain. He has no hemoptysis. He has no abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea or blood per rectum. Other than the ankle pain, he has no other joint involvement. He denies parasthesias and has no limb weakness. He does not have symptoms consistent with Raynauld’s phenomenon or digital ischemia. On exam, his vitals are stable. He has leg edema to his knees. His rash in non-blancheable and painful to touch. It is worse around ankles and he has no lesions above knees. His ankles are swollen and warm. He has difficulty with both passive and active range of motion at the ankles. He can weight bear but has an antalgic gait. The rest of the exam was normal.

stem: What investigations should be ordered initially (check all that apply)
answer: The correct answers are A, B, C, D, E, F, G, I, J, N, O, and P. The CBC determines if the white count is elevated, which may suggest an infection and whether the hemoglobin is low and platelets high, which can be seen in inflammation from infection or autoimmune disease. Similarly, elevations in ESR and/or CRP tells us if there is systemic inflammation. It is important to ensure that there is no coagulopathy, which can cause purpura; thus, look for low platelets and/or elevated INR and PTT. ALT can be high and albumin low in liver dysfunction that can occur with some types of primary and secondary vasculitis. To rule out infections that commonly cause purpura, blood cultures, hepatitis and HIV should be tested (even in patients without risk factors; however, this patient does have risk factors, including prior i.v. drug use and tattoos). Given the prior use of i.v. drugs and because cocaine use can cause purpura, it should be discussed with the patient whether he consents to have a urine toxicology screen. The patient has ankle pain and swelling; thus, bilateral ankle X-rays should be performed to assess for evidence of arthritis. Because asymptomatic manifestations of vasculitis can occur in the lungs and kidney, it is important to obtain a serum creatinine, urinalysis and a chest X-ray in all patients suspected of vasculitis. A skin biopsy is helpful to confirm a diagnosis of vasculitis; however, it does not need to be performed with the initial investigations. Less invasive tests can sometimes identify the underlying cause making the skin biopsy unnecessary. It is also not recommended to perform a skin biopsy for non-severe (non-ulcerating) purpura with a duration of symptoms less than 4-6 weeks because often these resolve on their own and are due to unspecified viral infections or hypersensitivity reactions. The urine cultures do not need to be done unless the urinalysis shows evidence of infection, RF and ANCA do not need to be tested before the results of the other investigations. If the initial investigations do not identify a cause, serology for autoimmune disease can be considered depending on symptoms. In this case, the patient had evidence of inflammatory arthritis; therefore, ANA, RF and/or anti-CCP2 can be ordered. ANCA can be ordered by the specialist once secondary causes of vasculitis are ruled out. The patient has no respiratory or abdominal complaints; therefore, the CT scan is not indicated.

preamble.title: The case, continued
preamble.html: The case. The results revealed an elevated ALT of 70 (normal <30) and a CRP of 50 (normal <5). He had a positive anti-HCV antibody, suggesting a prior or current hepatitis C infection. The rest of his labs and X-Rays were normal. The treating physician contacted rheumatology on-call who advised that blood be sent for hepatitis C viral load and cryoglobulins. The rheumatologist explained that hepatitis C infection can directly cause vasculitis and inflammatory arthritis, or it can be associated with cyroglobulins that causes a small vessel vasculitis. Either way, the first-line treatment for the arthritis and purpura associated with hepatitis C is to treat the underlying infection with antivirals.

stem: The patient is very bothered by his rash and ankle pain and he is not getting relief from ibuprofen. What can be prescribed to relieve symptoms while the patient awaits the investigations? (select all that apply)

options.html: Another oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory (i.e. diclofenac, naproxen, etc.)

answer: The correct answers are A, D, E, and F. Acetaminophen is minimally effective for the pain of inflammatory arthritis and does not treat cutaneous vasculitis. There is no evidence for cannabinoids for this indication. Methotrexate takes a long time to start working; thus, it is not useful to manage acute symptoms. Given that this patient’s likely diagnosis is an underlying infection (hepatitis C), methotrexate which is an immunosuppressant that can also cause liver toxicity should not be used. In other patients who have primary cutaneous vasculitis, methotrexate can be used for non-resolving, scarring or severe skin disease. Topical corticosteroids can be used first line for non-severe cutaneous vasculitis. If it is not effective, NSAIDs can be tried in patients that do not have contraindications. Another anti-inflammatory is colchicine and it can be used for cutaneous vasculitis and arthritis (0.6 mg twice a day with dose adjusted for renal disease) with the major side effect being diarrhea. Oral corticosteroids are very effective for cutaneous vasculitis and arthritis; however, there are significant side effects, and should be avoided if possible. If other agents fail, infection has been ruled out and the skin disease is severe, moderate doses of prednisone can be used with taper (30 mg for 1 week then decrease by 5 mg every 5 days until off).

stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with new right-sided headache and pain and stiffness in her shoulders and hips that is worse in the morning and improves with activity. She has been very fatigued but has no other symptoms. She weighs 70 kg. What is the initial management plan (select all that apply):

options.html: Urgent laboratory investigations (CBC, Creatinine, ALT, ESR, CRP and a urinalysis) to be performed at this clinic visit.
Urgent referral for temporal artery biopsy
Start prednisone 50 mg daily after the results of the laboratory investigations are available and only if the ESR or CRP is elevated
Start prednisone 50 mg daily after the results of the laboratory investigations and temporal artery biopsy are available and only if the ESR or CRP is elevated
Start prednisone 50 mg daily after the results of the laboratory investigations and temporal artery biopsy are available and only if the biopsy is consistent with GCA
Start calcium, vitamin D and a proton pump inhibitor to protect from steroid side effects

answer: The correct answers are A, B, D, H, and J. GCA should be suspected in this patient because she has new onset headache and symptoms that would be consistent with PMR, which is frequently associated with GCA. It is critical to test for ESR and CRP immediately to ensure accuracy of the test. A negative ESR and CRP in a patient who is not on steroids, makes GCA very unlikely. After the blood is drawn for the inflammation markers, the patient should be started immediately on high dose steroids (1 mg/ kg daily to maximum of 60 mg daily); a delay in starting steroids can lead to severe complications, such as blindness and/or stroke. If the blood cannot be drawn immediately, then the steroid should be started, and the laboratory investigations completed as soon as possible. It is important to confirm the diagnosis with a temporal artery biopsy; however, steroid treatment should not be delayed waiting for the biopsy to be performed. Because steroids have serious side effects, particularly in the elderly: calcium and vitamin D should be started to prevent fractures and a proton pump inhibitor to prevent gastritis and peptic ulcer disease. It is not necessary to start a bisphosphonate for bone protection immediately; this can be started later after the diagnosis is confirmed. All patients with GCA should be referred to rheumatology or another specialist with an interest in GCA (could be general medicine, neurology, ophthalmology) for confirmation of diagnosis, additional medical management and monitoring).

preamble.title: The case - joint pain after a non-resolving sinus infection
preamble.html:
The case. 55 year old woman presents with joint pain and swelling. You had been following her for the last 2 months for a non-resolving sinus infection for which she had already received 2 courses of antibiotics. She did not have fevers but felt chills. The symptoms of her sinus infection were facial pain, frontal headache, nasal congestion, purulent discharge and nasal crusting. In the last week she was also complaining of epistaxis and right ear fullness with hearing loss. A CT of her sinuses showed opacification of her sinuses. You had referred her to ENT, but the appointment was pending. The joint pain and swelling came on subacutely a week ago. It involved the wrists, right knee, left ankle and some of her PIPs. Her symptoms were worse in the morning and associated with 1 hour of morning stiffness. Her symptoms improved with ibuprofen. She is not any other medications, does not have any past medical history and her cancer screening is up to date. She has no significant family history. She does not drink, smoke or use any drugs or herbals. She works as a PSW and has travelled to the Philippines.

She has felt terrible the last several months with no energy and decreased appetite. She has lost 10 kg. She denies dyspnea but has not been active. She has some mild cough, worse in the morning and she feels it dripping down from her nose. She has no chest pain and no abdominal complaints. She denies any ocular complaints. She has no parasthesias and no focal weakness. On physical exam, the patient’s vitals are stable and she is afebrile. She is not in respiratory distress. She has tenderness over her sinuses. The tympanic membrane on the left was cloudy and bulging. She had several swollen tender joints. The rest of the exam was non-contributory. You had sent basic laboratory investigations and found that she was anemic with a hemoglobin of 100, platelets and WBC were slightly elevated at 520 and 13, respectively. Her liver enzymes and creatinine were normal. CRP was 80 (normal <5)

stem: What additional investigations should be ordered? (click all that apply)

options.html: Biopsy of sinonasal tissue to send for pathology and culture

answer: The correct answers are A, B, D, F, I, J, and O. The patient has non-resolving sinusitis with inflammatory arthritis and systemic symptoms. The differential diagnosis includes an infection, vasculitis, sarcoidosis or lymphoma. She could also have two processes occurring - a resistant/atypical sinus infection and causes of inflammatory arthritis (RA, lupus, CPPD, etc.). Blood cultures are important to assess for systemic infection. Sputum cultures are low yield and usually contaminated with oral flora. Given her travel history, a TB skin test is indicated. She does not have risk factors for HIV, but it can cause the patients symptoms and would be recommended to test for it. Vasculitis and lupus can be asymptomatic in the lungs and kidneys; therefore, the patient should have a urinalysis and chest X-Ray. The CT chest and PFTs do not need to be ordered right away but can be considered if the chest X-ray is normal because it is difficult to assess for dyspnea given the low activity level. The patient has evidence of inflammatory arthritis; thus, RF/anti-CCP2 and ANA should be ordered. Anti-ENA should only be done if ANA is positive. The complement levels are non-specific and do not need to be ordered unless ANA is positive and there is concern for lupus. ANCA would be helpful, but it is not reimbursed. It can be ordered once infectious and other causes are ruled out. There is concern for autoimmune disease, a biopsy of the sinuses is necessary to rule out atypical infections such as fungal and TB before starting immunosuppressive agents.

preamble.title: The case, continued
preamble.html: The case. The investigations showed negative blood cultures and TB skin test. Her HIV, ANA, RF and anti-CCP2 were negative. A chest X-Ray showed multiple cavitary lesions and the urinalysis showed blood and protein.

stem: What is the differential diagnosis?
answer: The correct answers are A, C, D, E, F, and G. The patient is ANA negative, which would make lupus highly unlikely. Similarly, rheumatoid vasculitis generally does not occur in patients who are RF negative. The patient’s investigations were concerning for renal disease and she also had cavitary lesions in her lungs. These findings are non-specific and can be seen in GPA, infections and cancer. TB is not ruled out because there are false negatives with TB skin tests.

stem: The patient has multi-organ involvement and the cause is not yet identified, as a primary care provider, what is the next step?

options.html: Arrange for the patient to be admitted to hospital
Call nephrology for an urgent referral
Send the patient for further investigations to identify the underlying cause
Wait for the ENT appointment before taking further action
Call ENT to update on patient status and inquire about a more urgent appointment
Refer to rheumatology and respirology for an urgent assessment

answer: The correct answers are B, F, and G. The patient is stable with no respiratory distress and her creatinine is normal; it is not necessary for urgent admission at this time. However, the patient needs to be monitored closely and she should be advised to go to the emergency department if she develops serious symptoms (i.e. dyspnea, hemoptysis, chest pain, fevers, syncope, vision loss, severe headache, focal neurologic signs, etc.). Her most pressing issue is the evidence of renal dysfunction with proteinuria and hematuria because she is at risk for rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Therefore, nephrology should be contacted urgently. It would not be appropriate to wait for the pending ENT visit as the patient has multi-organ involvement and needs rapid assessment by other specialties. However, since the patient has already been referred to ENT and a sinonasal biopsy would be helpful to assist with diagnosis, it would be beneficial to contact ENT with an update on the patient’s condition and request a more urgent appointment. In addition, given that vasculitis is on the differential and that the patient has lung involvement, rheumatology and respirology should be consulted. It is not necessary for the primary care physician to initiate further investigations at this point as the specialty providers can manage going forward. It would also not be advisable to start high dose prednisone before evaluation by specialty care because infection remains on the differential and corticosteroids can worsen infections.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: 14 y.o. male. Acute onset right hip pain while participating in 100m dash at school track meet. Antalgic limp, anterior hip pain. Hip radiographs are taken.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is B. The reveal follows the case: "Avulsion Fractures - can occur at any apophysis; bones growing fast, muscle/tendon under tension - quick burst of activity/contraction pulls it off! Common: pelvis, 5th MT, medial epicondyle; treatment is often non-surgical." A sudden burst (a sprint) giving acute anterior hip pain in a growing teenager is that mechanism, at the pelvis. Overuse apophysitis (A) is the gradual-onset traction injury the notes turn to next (Osgood-Schlatter, Sinding-Larsen, Sever's), not an acute event. Osteochondritis dissecans (C) is a repetitive-movement loss of blood flow under the articular cartilage, not a sudden injury at a tendon attachment. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (D) is listed among the hip causes of a limp, and is not what this case is teaching.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Case - 15 mos with LLD. Pelvic radiographs are shown.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? (the lecture poses no question here. The diagnosis is the section the case sits in, developmental dysplasia of the hip)

options.html: Growth arrest after a Salter-Harris V injury

answer: The correct answer is C. The case sits inside the developmental dysplasia of the hip section, between the Ortolani test and "DDH Management". A leg length discrepancy is one of the exam findings the lecture lists for it (Galeazzi test), and at 15 months the Barlow and Ortolani tests are no longer reliable ("unreliable > 3-6 months old"), so the hip was not caught by them. At this age the management is no longer the Pavlik harness (up to 6 months) but closed reduction and spica cast, or open reduction ± osteotomies. Physiologic genu varum (A) is normal from birth to 2 years and is symmetric; asymmetry is one of its warning signs. Growth arrest after a Salter-Harris V injury (B) can cause a leg length discrepancy, but there is no injury here. Plastic deformation (D) is a bowing fracture after trauma.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Case 1. 33 year old ♂ with back/flank mass. History: noticed 6 years ago; "big"; not quite doubled in size; uncomfortable; multiple other lumps; has an uncle with lumps. Physical exam: obvious mass; skin over intact, normal; "big"; in subcutaneous tissues; easily mobile; other lesions, obvious lipomas.

stem: What Do You Do Next?

options.html: Excisional biopsy with minimal surrounding tissue
Imaging (MRI preferred) or a surgical expert
Reassure as a lipoma, no further workup

answer: The correct answer is C. The lecture answers with its guideline: a mass > 5 cm goes to imaging (MRI preferred, CT, rarely ultrasound) or a surgical expert, then biopsy, whatever its other features. "Big" here is 17 × 16 × 5 cm on the ultrasound that follows: "probable lipoma, cannot rule out sarcoma, recommend MRI... or referral to surgeon familiar with soft-tissue tumors." Excision (A) is only for a mass < 5 cm with no suspicious features, and an excisional biopsy is "not ideal if sarcoma". Fine needle aspiration (B) is not widely used for primary diagnosis: poor cell yield, hard to tell tumour types apart. Reassuring (D) is the "whoops" the lecture warns about: a lump assumed benign that turns out to be a sarcoma.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Case 1, continued. The mass is excised. On pathology there are fat cells with spindle and multinucleated cells. Immunohistochemistry is MDM2 negative and CD34 positive.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? (follow-up assembled from the case notes, which pose no question here)
answer: The correct answer is B. The notes give the differential for fat with spindle and multinucleated cells: benign spindle cell/pleomorphic lipoma (observe) versus malignant well-differentiated liposarcoma (atypical lipomatous tumour), and resolves it with immunohistochemistry: "MDM2 negative and CD34 positive -> lipoma" (the result is labelled spindle cell/pleomorphic lipoma). Well-differentiated liposarcoma (A) is the alternative that MDM2 negativity rules out. Dedifferentiated liposarcoma (C) is case 4's diagnosis, shown with MDM2 staining. Myxoid liposarcoma (D) shows lipoblasts, uniform oval cells, branching capillaries and a myxoid stroma.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Case 2. 18 year old ♂ brought in by his mother with right hip mass. History: noticed 18 mos ago? no change?; no trauma; asymptomatic; no other lumps; no family history. Physical exam: obvious mass; skin over intact, normal; size of small plum; in subcutaneous tissues; tethered; nodes clear.

stem: What Next?

options.html: Reassure, and review the mass in clinic in a year
Excise it, since it is under 5 cm and asymptomatic
Fine needle aspiration, then excise if it is benign

answer: The correct answer is D. The notes answer with their guideline and then show the imaging and "Management - Case 2: Biopsy; discussion at multidisciplinary tumor board". A plum is under 5 cm, but this mass is tethered, and "fixed" is one of the suspicious features (rapid growth, pain, recurrent, deep, fixed, difficult location). A mass < 5 cm with a suspicious feature goes to imaging (MRI preferred, CT, rarely ultrasound) or a surgical expert before biopsy. B applies only to a mass < 5 cm with no suspicious features. C uses fine needle aspiration, which is not widely used for primary diagnosis. A ignores the suspicious feature.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Case 3. 55 year old ♂ left thigh mass, neurofibromatosis. History: noticed past year; now a football, more than doubled in size; dull ache last 2-3 months, takes voltaren, continues to work; neurofibromatosis. Physical exam: obvious mass quadriceps; skin over intact, normal; size of cantaloupe; in muscle, tethered; no inguinal lymphadenoapthy. An MRI of the mass and a core biopsy are done.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? (the lecture asks "What Next?" and answers it with its guideline; this asks for the diagnosis it gives instead, leaving it out of the stem)
answer: The correct answer is A. The lecture: "Sarcoma arising in the setting of neurofibromatosis, consistent with malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour." Neurofibromatosis is a genetic predisposition to sarcoma (neurofibromin mutation), and the mass has every suspicious feature on the lecture's guideline: > 5 cm, more than doubled in a year, painful, deep (in muscle) and tethered. Neurofibroma (C) is the benign peripheral nerve tumour in the nomenclature table, and benign tumours have limited growth. A well-differentiated liposarcoma (B) is a fatty tumour (case 1's malignant alternative), not one arising from nerve in neurofibromatosis. Rhabdomyosarcoma (D) is the malignant skeletal muscle tumour, one of the pediatric sarcomas.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Case 4. 55 year old ♂ with abdominal mass. History: ER visit for paresthesia's; ↑ abdominal girth; ↓ appetite, early satiety; 20 lb weight loss; N bowel movements; fatigue; otherwise well; no family hx. A CT scan shows a very large abdominal mass.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is D. The lecture: "no biopsy needed - all agreed liposarcoma" from the CT; it then names it a dedifferentiated liposarcoma (on MDM2 staining) and contrasts it with a well-differentiated liposarcoma, which recurs locally but does not metastasize distantly and can progress to a dedifferentiated liposarcoma, which can. ⚠ The lecture makes the final call between those two on pathology after resection; from the history and CT alone the lecture gets as far as "liposarcoma", which is why only one liposarcoma is offered. Rhabdomyosarcoma (C) is the malignant skeletal muscle tumour, one of the pediatric sarcomas. A spindle cell/pleomorphic lipoma (B) is benign, case 1's diagnosis. A malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (A) is case 3's, a thigh sarcoma in neurofibromatosis.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Let's Review a Case! Open fracture. Distal 1/3 tibial diaphysis. Spiral. Mild displacement: shortened, posterior translation, apex lateral angulation.

stem: What to do??

options.html: IV cefazolin, tetanus prophylaxis, early debridement, irrigation and an intramedullary nail
Closed reduction and a cast, then antibiotics and tetanus only if a wound infection develops
Splint and elevate, then delayed surgery and wound closure once the swelling has settled
Irrigate the wound in the emergency room, close it, and treat the fracture as a closed one

answer: The correct answer is A. The lecture works the case: early antibiotics (2 g IV cefazolin); tetanus prophylaxis, given in the emergency room; early surgery, removing all devitalized tissue including bone fragments, gently irrigating with sterile saline, and stabilizing with an intramedullary nail; and early closure of the soft tissue envelope where possible (minimal contamination plus minimal debridement = direct closure during the open reduction and internal fixation). The goal is to convert an unstable contaminated wound into a stable clean environment. B waits for infection instead of giving early antibiotics, and a cast is not the definitive stabilization here. C delays the surgery and the closure that the lecture wants early. D treats an open fracture as closed, when any fracture with a wound is open until proven otherwise and needs operative debridement.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Source: Fracture Management and Complications Part 1.pdf slides 12-14 and Part 3.pdf slide 9 (2 cases). Tests 07 - Fracture Management. Part 3 slide 9.
stem: Sooo...tibial fracture with increasing narcotic requirements, terrible pain, pain increases with dorsiflexion or plantar flexion. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is D. This is the lecture's compartment syndrome picture: a clinical diagnosis of pain out of proportion to the injury and pain with passive stretch of the muscle involved in the compartment, then paresthesia (midterm), paralysis (very late) and pulselessness (not typical). The lower leg is the most common site, and a tibial fracture bleeds and swells inside fixed fascial borders. It is an urgent call to orthopedics: remove casts and dressings, elevate, cool, monitor, and definitive fasciotomy. Deep vein thrombosis (A) is a thromboembolic complication from Virchow's triad, not pain on moving the foot. Heterotopic ossification (B) is ectopic bone around a joint, presenting as stiffness. Avascular necrosis (C) occurs in bones with a retrograde blood supply: femoral head, talus, scaphoid, not the tibia.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (2 questions). Tests [[07 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A patient has repeat X-rays done 7 days after sustaining a distal radius fracture for which she underwent a closed reduction and casting. The fracture actually looks slightly wider than it did initially. The patient is doing well clinically, there is no new pain at the site. The alignment of the fracture fragments is otherwise unchanged (ie. no new angulation or translation). What is the most likely explanation for this finding?
answer: The correct answer is C. It’s too early to identify nonunion, and infection is unlikely in this closed fracture in a clinically well person. The reduction appears to be maintained given the absence of new deformity at the site. Most likely, the fracture line appears slightly widened due to the normal bony resorption that occurs in early fracture healing.

stem: 68F "Nancy". Sedentary, used to walk her dog on nearby trails. Worried about falling. HPI: Hypertension (140/85) – newly diagnosed and untreated. Family hx – father MI at 70, mother hip # at 73. How would you write a physical activity Rx? Consider benefits, side effects, risks… dose? (rewritten as MCQ: which screening and advice fits her risk?)

options.html: Supervised start or exercise specialist referral

answer: C - begin with low/moderate intensity exercise. Reasoned from the lecture's stratification: Nancy is asymptomatic with a significant risk factor (raised blood pressure, the table's own example), which is row 2: "Begin with low/moderate intensity exercise". She has no symptoms of cardiovascular disease (so not D's or B's rows), and her blood pressure of 140/85 is well under the absolute contraindication of resting SBP > 180 or DBP > 100. On the ACSM screening she is not a regular exerciser with no signs or symptoms, which also leads to light-to-moderate intensity. Self-directed activity (A) is for asymptomatic, low-risk patients without significant risk factors. The family history is not in the lecture's stratification, so the lecture does not say whether it moves her up a row; that is left to the session.

stem: 68F "Nancy". Sedentary, used to walk her dog on nearby trails. Worried about falling. HPI: Hypertension (140/85) – newly diagnosed and untreated. Family hx – father MI at 70, mother hip # at 73. How would you write a physical activity Rx? Consider benefits, side effects, risks… dose? (rewritten as MCQ: which prescription fits?)

options.html: Heavy resistance training 3x/week, 30 minutes, with overhead lifts
Running 5x/week, 30 minutes, so hard that talking is impossible
No exercise until her blood pressure is controlled with medication
Walking 5x/week, 30 minutes, at a talk-but-not-sing pace

answer: D. Reasoned from the lecture's F.I.T.T. framework: frequency 5x per week, intensity moderate (can talk but not sing), time 30 minutes, type aerobic such as walking - and she used to walk her dog, which suits her preferences. For hypertension the lecture adds a prolonged warm-up (15 min) and cool-down (10 min), and lists very strenuous resistance training and overhead exercises as DON'Ts (A). Sedentary patients should start low and go slow, and her stratification row begins at low/moderate intensity, not vigorous (B). Only BP > 180/100 must be controlled with medication before exercise (C); hers is 140/85. Strength and balance work twice a week would also address her fear of falling, but no option turns on it.

stem: A 32 year-old woman presents with alopecia, malar rash, oral ulceration, pleurisy, and swollen MCP and PIP joints. Blood work comes back positive for ANA 1:640 with a speckled pattern, positive double-stranded DNA, and low complement. A diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus is made and you have decided to start prednisone and hydryoxychloroquine. You discuss potential benefits and adverse effects of the medication. Which of the following are not side effects of prednisone?

options.html: All of the above are side effects of prednisone

answer: The correct answer is D. Prednisone increases the risk of infection. All of the other answers are potential complications of prednisone. Prednisone is a good treatment option to treat acute inflammation, but is not good long-term due to potential complications.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (10 questions). Tests [[03 - Rheumatology Treatments]].
stem: A 75 year-old gentleman presents with a 2-day history of a red, swollen, exquisitely tender 1st MTP joint. He has a medical history consisting of end-stage renal disease, congestive heart failure requiring diuretic use, and poorly controlled diabetes. He drinks approximately 20 beers per week. Blood work shows elevated inflammatory markers and a normal urate. Synovial fluid aspiration of the MTP joint shows intracellular monosodium urate crystals, a cell count of 17.1 x 109, and negative culture and Gram stain. Which of following is the best treatment option of acute gout in this patient?

options.html: Oral prednisone 30 mg daily x 3 days, followed by taper

answer: The correct answer is B. Given this patient’s comorbidities, the best treatment option for acute gout affecting one joint would be intra-articular steroids. Intra-articular steroids have minimal systemic absorption. Prednisone is relatively contraindicated due to his heart failure and diabetes, both of which can worsen with prednisone. NSAIDs should be avoided in patients with end-stage renal disease.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (10 questions). Tests [[03 - Rheumatology Treatments]].
stem: A clinical clerk is rotating through an elective block in rheumatology and asked to obtain informed consent for joint aspiration for a 55 year-old gentleman presenting with acute monoarthritis of the right knee. After discussing potential benefits, the student then discusses potential complications of the procedure. Which of the following are not complications of arthrocentesis (joint aspiration)?

options.html: All of the above are complications of joint aspiration

answer: The correct answer is D. Post injection flare and minimal systemic absorption of prednisone that can worsen hyperglycemia are complications of steroid injection, not joint aspiration - which does not involve injection of cortisone. Infection, bleeding, and tendon rupture are potential complications of inserting the needle, but are rare in clinical practice.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (10 questions). Tests [[03 - Rheumatology Treatments]].
stem: A 65 year-old woman with a history of gastritis presents to clinic for suggestions regarding pain control for her hand osteoarthritis. She has previously tried occupational therapy, topical NSAIDs, acetaminophen, and glucosamine chondroitin with limited improvement of her symptoms. She wonders about trying an anti-inflammatory but is concerned about potential worsening of her gastritis. Which of the following NSAIDs has the least risk of GI toxicity?
answer: The correct answer is B. Due to its selective inhibition of COX-2, celecoxib is associated with less GI toxicity than non-selective NSAIDs (i.e., all other available NSAIDs). Celecoxib can still result in gastritis and peptic ulcer disease and should be used with caution in this patient, possibly with a proton pump inhibitor.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics

stem: A 45 year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has recently been referred to your rheumatology clinic. She has been taking hydroxychloroquine 400 mg PO daily for twenty years since she was initially diagnosed with lupus. Her disease is currently under control. She has not had any recent eye exam. What is the retinal finding of hydroxychloroquine that you would be concerned about?
answer: The correct answer is D. Bull’s eye maculopathy is a toxic retinopathy caused by hydroxychloroquine. It is important to tell patients about the potential complication when starting this medication and ensure they are getting annual eye exams to monitor for this complication.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (10 questions). Tests [[03 - Rheumatology Treatments]].
stem: A 45 year-old gentleman with psoriatic arthritis on sulfasalazine presents to your clinic after developing a new skin rash. He reports a itchy, red rash on his arms and torso that started 2 weeks ago. He has had some relief of the pruritis with anti-histamines. He continues to have a raised, erythematous, urticarial rash on exam. He asks if it is caused by his sulfasalazine. Which of the following are not potential side effects of sulfasalazine?
answer: The correct answer is F. Acute pneumonitis (shortness of breath, cough, fever) is not associated with sulfasalazine, but rather methotrexate and less commonly leflunomide. This patient has a pruritic, erythematous rash with an urticarial appearance that is consistent with a drug rash. Both sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine can cause drug rashes. This patient should avoid sulfa drugs in the future.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (10 questions). Tests [[03 - Rheumatology Treatments]].
stem: A 45 year-old gentleman with psoriatic arthritis is about to start a TNF inhibitor for his skin and joint disease. Which of the following is not a contraindication to starting a TNF inhibitor.
answer: The correct answer is C. So long as patients do not have advance congestive heart failure, coronary artery disease is not a contraindication to starting biologic therapy with a TNF inhibitor. The rest of the conditions listed are relative or absolute contraindications to starting TNF inhibitors.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (10 questions). Tests [[03 - Rheumatology Treatments]].
stem: A 24 year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is being worked up for biologic therapy after failing sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine. She wants to avoid using methotrexate and leflunomide because she wants to conceive in the near future. She has a family history of multiple sclerosis. Which class of biologic therapy should she avoid?
answer: The correct answer is B. Due to potential for demyelinating disease, TNF inhibitors are avoided in patients with a personal or family history of multiple sclerosis. The other classes of biologics do not cause this. There is limited data available for some of the newer biologic medications and pregnancy, so the patient should be made aware about this before trying to conceive.
